title: How to Paint Everything: Horrible Flesh Textures for Trench Crusade
content:
The art of Trench Crusade pushes the boundaries of grimdark through the use of textures we usually rely on model sculpts to achieve. Flayed skin, open wounds, rotting flesh, seeping blood - it's all found on just about every page of the Trench Crusade core book, but when it comes to modelling we're usually dependent on the kindness (or warpedness) of a particular sculptor to see them on our models. I don't think that's right - not for something as steeped in Catholic ideas of the mortification of the flesh, at least - for Trench Crusade. So I've been experimenting with ways you can up your grimdark painting game in colours, textures and effects. This has all been done mainly with an eye for painting up Heretic Naval Raiders for the forthcoming Carcass Front starter set, but it works just about everywhere. In a world where sentient plague flies sink their proboscis deep into the brains of saints, and living flesh is warped into horrible umbilici that pipe fevered dreams of gluttony and lust into the souls of the faithful, why the hell are we relying on boring old paint to do the job?

This is the last technique talked about in this article, but it's gone well enough I'm going to show it here. Horrible Flesh Textures

Before we dive in, there is - of course - another content warning. Just like last time, and the time before that [Editor's Note: This is your warning that this is the toe tank link], the idea here is to create something that looks disgusting. The highlight of this process has been that several of the photos were flagged on Discord as sensitive content - what an honour for a grimdark painter - but Norman says it's chill, so here we go!

Rotting Flesh

There’s a lot of contexts in trench crusade where you want rotting skin in varying amounts. Terrain, trench pilgrims, any and all demon factions, takwin monstrosities, the list goes on, and that’s not even mentioning the entire rotting flesh faction. So, something that looks altogether more putrid than a green wash over light tones is much needed. Multi layered rotting flesh is time consuming but it looks fantastic - but isn’t quite as slow as you might think.

The idea is to add multiple layers of very thin paint in irregular shapes, building up a blotchy, multicoloured set of colours that mimic rotting flesh really well by selling the illusion of depth and rot acting on different layers of organ and skin. Between each layer, add some form of protection for the previous one, and repeat this until you’re satisfied.

There are two ways you can do the technique presented here but both of them end up the same way. The model example uses both - on (stage) left, acrylic washes, on (stage) right, isopropyl alcohol. I don’t recommend the iso method - it’s poisonous, headachey and a solution in search of a problem. The idea with using iso is that it can reduce the surface tension of paint allowing it to bloom across a low-friction surface. The exact same effect (science!) is achievable by putting a drop of hand soap in your paint water, so do that instead.

Step by Step Rotting Flesh

Prepare your model by painting the skin areas in two very light, similar tones. I used dark arts altar ivory over an off white primer. Lighter the better here, and don’t worry about using a skin tone.

Our big ogre with the first blotchy colours. Horrible Flesh Textures

Next, add a thin blotch of watery paint. Shades, Inks, Contrast all work well. I used the following colours in rotation across the remainder of the process:

  • Citadel Druchii Violet
  • Citadel Ultramar Blue Contrast
  • Citadel Snakebite Leather Contrast
  • A Citadel Purple Shade/Wash whose label has long since worn off
  • Dark Arts Brown Ink
  • Army Painter Dry Blood
  • Army Painter True Blood

The yellow is a little different as, after many years of trying, I've found that all yellows sold by everyone aren't quite right for me. Instead, it's a teaspoon of tumeric mixed into Army Painter Stabiliser (acrylic medium). The nice thing about this is that it goes on very very yellow, then fades with exposure to sunlight, giving you auto-shadow-and-highlight, as well as being easy to remove and paint over. The whole model reeks of tumeric after, too, which might be a positive or negative thing depending on how you feel.

Before that paint dries (count to ten seconds), use a fine brush with soapy water (or iso) on it to agitate the blotch roughly. Aim for an irregular fringed shape. Some of the paint will have dried to a fine crusty line, while the rest will bloom across the skin in its own way. Don’t try to control this, just let it go! Do this in a couple of places across the model but don’t overdo it - leave plenty of base tone showing.

First colour Layer - Horrible Flesh Textures

Next, add a layer of protection that will (slightly) repel paint - brush on, airbrush or rattle can gloss and satin varnish works, if you’re using ISO use superglue, or a very very thin layer of PVA. If using PVA give it at least a couple of hours drying time.

After a few coats. Horrible Flesh Textures

 

Then repeat the paint/bloom process using other colours. Keep the paint watery - past milk texture into squash levels of dilution. Once dry, add another layer of protection.

Really getting there now! Horrible Flesh Textures

You can repeat this infinitely, though three layers will give you a fantastically deep, rich look. Changing the colours from darker to lighter looks good too, but there are no rules here - experiment and see what you come up with!

Transparent Skin

Once you’re happy with the colour pattern you’ve created with your decaying flesh, it’s time to make it look pellucid, creepy and horrifying. This is incredibly simple - the magic of PVA!

A thick layer. Horrible Flesh Textures

Once all the paint is totally and completely dry, add a relatively thick layer (primer layer thickness is fine) of PVA all over the model. Once that’s dry, use a fine brush and trace the occasional blood vessel (dark blood, black or purple works best) over it.

Add another layer of PVA, this time with a very, very small amount of your base light tone added in, and a little water to help it mix. You want the mixture to look like this:

Mixed PVA and Paint Horrible Flesh Textures

And you’ll need a fair bit of it, because you want to do at least two layers of it! This forms a horribly translucent, semi-realistic glaze of both a skinlike texture and colour over your blooming bruises and haemorrhages, and the more layers the better. Once you’re done, don’t throw that mix out - spread it out over a shallow container and leave it for later.

Horrible Flesh Textures

The water added in also means that the drying PVa will pull tighter than usual across the model, which can pull up some delightful textures.  If you want a bit more skin tone over your rot, add another layer rather than more paint, you don’t want to obscure all your hard, disgusting work.

Open Sores and Wounds

The multiple layers of PVA we've added to the skin allows us to create incredible looking wound effects with nothing more than a pin and a few washes. Scrape a pin or modelling knife across (horizontally at first) where you'd like to add a wound.

Dragging some holes into it. Horrible Flesh Textures

Tease the edges of the PVA into the shape you'd like, and firmly press down on the wound once it's in the shape and size you want.

Establishing some ragged shapes. Horrible Flesh Textures

Moving quickly, use a small brush to flick watered down paint - try blood effects, black washes, or deep purples - under the edges of the open wound. The paint should wick up under one or more layers of PVA, creating a subtle bloom and adding depth to the effect.

Horrible Flesh Textures

Whack on another very thin coat of PVA to hold any trailing bits of skin in place, and to stop them catching and peeling further.

Once all that's dry, add a darker tone (brown works, though dried blood is also good), then a lighter one (bright blood, flesh or green). Agitate this mix with a pin, and rake up the lower layers of PVA while you're at it. If you'd like to expose bare muscle, do so in a pattern (vertical or horizontal stripes), while if you want liquified flesh bursting out just mix it up!

Now that's grim dark! Horrible Flesh Textures

You can return to the raised flaps of skin with a little highlight colour (Altar Ivory again in this case) if you wish, but go very easy and light on it as a major part of why this technique looks so grim is that the PVA retains its transparency. There's an immense amount of fun you can have with this technique. Ragged holes look rotted or torn (amazing for tooth and claw damage!), while taking your time to roll the PVA away from the area looks like sloughing skin or - and I haven't tried this yet - you could go really big with it. Ever heard of degloving?

You can see a first try at degloving on the belly wound. Horrible Flesh Textures

Flayed or Peeling Skin

One of the most metal pieces of devotional art in the world is in St Barts-the-Great Church in central London. St Bartholomew, the flayed saint, was often depicted in medieval art holding his own skin and flensing knife, which is generally very cool looking, and his statue in St Bart’s the lesser is a modern phenomenal rendition of it:

Whatever you think about Hirst, this absolutely rocks. Via Wikipedia

I wanted to do so thing similar for Trench pilgrims, but unfortunately plastic sculpted flayed skin always universally looks shite. It’s too think (the skin on flayed ones, to scale, would be a good couple of inches thick), it’s too plasticky and it’s usually too rigid. This is trench crusade so we want better (worse?) for our models.

Making draped and flayed skin is fairly easy, and luckily it’s a byproduct of the PVA deep skin process. Remember when I said don’t throw out that PVA and paint mix? If you’ve left it to dry naturally it should look something like this:

Dried PVA flesh. Horrible Flesh Textures

Pick a hole in that and drop a little water on the hole. It’ll run underneath the pva - once you’ve done that leave it again until it’s dry. Add a skin tone layer to the top - I’ve sponged on a very light mix of dark arts masque flesh and altar ivory and, if so inclined, freehand on some tattoo shapes and/or scars. This is going to be your skin to drape artfully wherever it’s needed.

When dry to the touch, use a sharp modelling knife and cut lines into the skin surface. This allows you to pull away strips rather than patches. You can cut around a whole shape or just two/three sides. The more you cut the more even the final result will be. Pull the pieces out with tweezers very carefully.

You can see the pieces end up very fine, which is ideal! Horrible Flesh Textures

There will be a lot of stretch and movement in each piece of skin, so you can drape, pull, roughen and essentially do whatever you like with them! They work great on models and slightly less well on banners and decoration. With two points of contact between model and skin, the pieces won’t curl up too much - if you’re going for single point of contact they won’t stay looking as they do for long. Attach them with pva and paint the interior side with your choice of horrible blood, gore, slime and rot effects. Paint on both sides helps rigidity, strength and longevity, as well as looking awesome.

Use at least two points of contact and the PVA skin will drape beautifully. Horrible Flesh Textures

While not as fragile as they look due to elasticity, They will remain much easier to damage than plastic, so handle with care.

Now That's Grim Dark!

There's a lot more to go here with the Drowned Metachrist, but here he is so far! Horrible Flesh Textures

Using these techniques is incredibly simple, and adds a whole lot of horrifying, trench crusade appropriate texture. This isn't the kind of game where highlights, shadows and base coats do the job. If you're still here, get on it, get the PVA out, avoid the Isopropyl alcohol and bloody well go for it! Next time we'll be looking at hair, fur, scourgemarks, lice, flies and all the other horrible stuff you need to do trench crusade the way it could (and perhaps shouldn't!) be done.

title: Beyond the Black Library: John Sollitto's Scholarguard
content:
Image credit: John Sollitto

The Warhammer universe is forged by some of the sharpest minds in speculative fiction. But what do they create when they step outside Games Workshop’s sandbox? In Beyond the Black Library, we cast a keen eye on the different fictional sandboxes and original worlds our favorite creators build when they aren't writing for the Imperium or the Mortal Realms.

While my earliest exposure to Warhammer fiction was many years ago now (Dan Abnett's Eisenhorn Omnibus), for the past two years I have been absolutely marinading my brain in the grimdark. While I've taken the occasional detour, one of the fun side-effects is that when you come across something light-hearted and whimsical, it can shine like a beacon on a moonless night. Scholarguard proved to be a terrific palate-cleanser that I didn't know I'd needed, but came as a breath of fresh air.

Getting Cozy

Like any other consumer market, speculative fiction isn't immune to trends. The one we're currently weathering (for better or for worse) at the moment is the LitRPG phenomenon, with a deluge of stories ranging from inspiration to imitation riding the wave of success currently enjoyed by Matt Dinniman's Dungeon Crawler Carl. While Scholarguard has nothing in common with the adventures of Princess Donut's Royal Court, it does have some of the genetics of a contemporary trend that still has a bit of life in it: the cozy fantasy.

Exemplified by books like The House in the Cerulean Sea by T. J. Klune and Travis Baldree's Legends & Lattes, these stories tend to tack in the complete opposite direction of your more traditional epic fantasy and grimdark tales. They tend to have low-stakes plots that focus on the magically mundane, everyday life in a fantasy world, and often spend more time on interpersonal relationships over combat or the intrigues of politics. Baldree's story, for example, involves a grizzled orc adventurer hanging up her sword to open up a coffee shop that becomes a haven for the community. Low stakes for sure, but for many that's part of the charm. 

And while 'escort quests' tend to be the bane of MMO's like World of Warcraft, it's exactly the kind of low-stakes, character-driven story John Sollitto aimed for with Scholarguard.

The Story

The story centers on Hunter Harcutt, a young aspiring adventurer in Autumngate looking for his first real contract to get his foot in the door at the Adventurer's Guild. When an elven scholar named Ianthoris Embergleam turns up at the inn that Hunter is working at looking for an escort back to his home city of Riverhall a hundred kilometers way, Hunter thinks he's found just the job.

What seems a simple and straightforward journey turns out to be anything but, as the scholar has in his possession a very rare scroll. A very rare necromantic scroll, the kind that less savory and scrupulous types would kill to get their hands on. Embergleam came across it in an old bookstore and, recognizing it for what it was, vowed to see it safely back to the academy for safekeeping.

Naturally, his acquisition draws exactly that kind of less savory and scrupulous attention, and with thugs, assassins, and a criminal necromancer hot on their heels Hunter and Embergleam must race to Riverhall before their pursuers relieve them of their treasure- and quite possibly their lives.

Image credit: Veritas

About John

While this is naturally a fantasy tale, Black Library readers will likely be more familiar with Sollitto's work in the grim, dark future. To date he's penned a trio of Warhammer 40K stories that have been featured in various anthologies.

His debut story, Redemption Through Blood, was originally released as a digital short as part of 2024's Daughters of the Emperor Week. It then saw its print debut the following year in the Paragon of Faith and Other Stories anthology (review). That was followed by The Redoubt, a Guardsmen-verses-tau tale which was one of the three brand-new stories contained in Death and Duty: An Astra Militarum Anthology (review).

Finally, the terrific World Ablaze anthology (review) from earlier this year gave us Rok Crackers, putting a different group of Guardsmen- these being combat engineers- up against the greenskin menace inside one of their asteroid bases.

Beyond Warhammer, he's also written an anthology of his short stories, The Ones Who Remain, and has done extensive work in comics including writing for Veritas, Certifiable Investigations, and Circuit Champ.

Scholarguard, notes John, was inspired by old-school pulp fantasy as well as countless hours spent playing Dungeons & Dragons.

So given the pedigree, how does it hold up?

All The Small Things

As I joined Hunter and Embergleam on their trek, what stood out to me the most was the contrast I've seen in his Warhammer stories. I don't want to call it "growth" because I don't know the timeline of his work, but the contrast is certainly suggestive of an author much more comfortable in his powers. Don't get me wrong, I've liked Sollitto's small (but growing) body of Black Library tales, but in each review there's been something I pointed to in that story that I felt it might have used- and here in Scholarguard it was delivered in spades.

For example, take his most recent story, Rok Crackers. I had some pacing concerns here, noting in my review that while the tale had a terrific premise, "if I had any complaint, it was that there wasn't quite enough of it. At times I felt like I was listening to a podcast on 1.25 speed, the tale moving just a little too fast."

Scholarguard never drags; its sequences don't overstay their welcome. But there's a deliberate slowness to some of them that lets the reader enjoy the scene the same way you might linger at a painting in a museum that's caught your eye, enjoying all its fine details. Sollitto's novel plays these to great effect, and that's where some of the 'cozy' feeling can come from.

In one of the book's best moments, the pair of heroes find shelter in a cottage in the woods that's been overtaken by nature, its original inhabitant long deceased. As Hunter explores this house that was once a home, Sollitto pulls the reader into the scene's fine details, drawing an almost affectionate portrait of the original owner. He reflects over the burial plot in the yard1, discovers the original owner's tranche of charcoal and sketchbooks filled with Audubon-like depictions of nature, and stares at the stars in the sky through the holes in the slowly-collapsing roof as he goes to sleep. Upon waking, he even attempts a sketch of a nearby bird himself. It's a wonderful respite from the story's action, as by now the intrepid duo have found they're being pursued.

It never feels overindulgent, but these details make the story shine and breathe with a richness of life.

Then reviewing The Redoubt, I noted that "a little more depth on our characters would not have been unwelcome." While it's undoubtedly true that the longer word count of a novel certainly affords greater opportunity for deep characterization than a short story, Sollitto uses the space well in particular with his main protagonist, Hunter. The story's premise- a an aspiring adventurer on his first quest- has plenty of opportunity to fall into the easy cliches of the genre.

Sollitto avoids the easy tropes, and does the actual work of building with depth. While Hunter does get into some swordfights, for instance, he's no young master swordsman with full metal plate-worthy plot armor. These skirmishes tack towards the realistic side- short, bloody affairs that carry only slightly less significant threat of injury to the victor as to the vanquished. For much of the story, Hunter has to balance the duty to push on with his quest with the physical toll his injuries and dwindling supplies are taking on him.

Indeed, there's just enough grit here to push the book outside the confines of YA fiction, but not so much that I couldn't easily recommend it to my older kids. The Hunter that ends the journey is a different young man than the one that started it, and by doing the work along the way it all feels very consistent.

Final Thoughts

If there's a place I did find the book a bit light, it was in its worldbuilding. Putting it simply, there really isn't much. With the exception of a few deities which have a light presence in the story, there's not a lot that made Scholarguard's world feel as alive and detailed as its inhabitants. It's all very standard-issue, generic fantasy-land with the usual D&D array of orcs, half-orcs, elves, half-elves, dwarves, and halflings. These distinctions are also largely cosmetic, with little impact on character or story, and if you rewrote it changing everyone to humans you wouldn't lose (or gain) a thing.

By the same token, it also means that we are spared the risk of what many over-eager aspiring worldbuilders do, liberally dolloping in the lore dumps on the reader like there's going to be a test at the end of the book. In the absence of a rich world or high-stakes plot, Sollitto leans on his characters and eye for painting the fine details to get the reader invested in the story, and in the main it he gets it right.

Ultimately, the main test for me of books like these comes down to, "would I read the next one?" In this case, I certainly would. If Sollitto continue to show the growth as a writer we're already seeing, I'll be delighted to see what he comes up with for Hunter's next adventure.

As for the Black Library, Scholarguard shows that Sollitto's can carry a novel, and while I'd never turn down seeing more of the grim, dark future it would be fun to see what he could do with the Age of Sigmar side of things. But if you're looking for a fun, pulpy fantasy novel with a delightful amount of depth, this one's worth a look!

Footnote

  1. Cemetry Gates by The Smiths came right to mind as I read this scene, showing the tone and mood Sollitto evoked here. It also shows my age.

title: The 25 best MTG cards of all time
content:
What are the best MTG cards ever made? There have been many, many Magic: The Gathering cards printed over the years, but most of them are destined to sit in dusty drawers, untouched and unloved. Not these all-stars. Here, we've drawn up a list of the most powerful and popular, old and new, from all of Magic: The Gathering's many formats.

We've looked back across countless MTG sets, from recent releases all the way back to Alpha, to find the coolest, most jaw-droppingly powerful cards in all of Magic: The Gathering. Some of these can still be played in your MTG Arena decks, though several have also done time on an MTG banlist or two.

  1. Badgermole Cub - the best new card
  2. Sol Ring - the best Commander card
  3. Craterhoof Behemoth - the best go-wide finisher
  4. Gaea's Cradle - the best land you can actually play
  5. The One Ring - the best artifact
  6. Griselbrand - the best reanimator target
  7. Swords to Plowshares - the best targeted removal
  8. Urza's Saga - the most value from one land
  9. Lurrus of the Dream-Den - the strongest mechanic
  10. Pack Rat - A limited powerhouse
  11. Oko, Thief of Crowns - the best planeswalker
  12. Contract From Below - technically disqualified
  13. Farewell - the best white board wipe
  14. Tinker - the best MTG tutor card
  15. Deathrite Shaman - the best mana dork MTG card
  16. Brainstorm - the best card draw spell
  17. Cyclonic Rift - the best blue boardwipe
  18. Mishra's Bauble - the best free spell
  19. The Meathook Massacre - the best black board wipe
  20. Teferi's Protection - the best protection spell
  21. Esper Sentinel - the best one drop
  22. Orcish Bowmasters - the best hate bear
  23. Blasphemous Act - the best red board wipe
  24. An Untapped Island - the scariest card to face

How we chose the best MTG cards

1. Badgermole Cub

The best new MTG card

When WotC added mythic rare cards to MtG in 2008, lead designer Mark Rosewater stated that the ideally, mythic rare cards would feel "very special and unique", "cards like Planeswalkers, most legends, and epic-feeling creatures and spells", and not just "each set's most powerful tournament-level cards."

Badgermole Cub, printed in Avatar: the Last Airbender, is a 2/2 for two mana, which turns one of your lands into a tiny creature, and means all of your mana dorks add an extra green mana whenever you tap them. It is an incredibly efficient mana accelerator that is seeing play as a four-of in Standard, Modern, Pioneer, Legacy, and Commander.

If this thing was a named legendary creature - even if it was a new version of that weird little rat Loot - it might feel like a mythic rare, purely on the basis that "cute little guys" is an established archetype for extremely rare and powerful creatures. As it stands, it feels like a rare from a Modern Horizons set that was mysteriously printed into Standard.

2. Sol Ring

The best Commander card

Next up we have a freebie. Sol Ring is the best Commander card in existence, and the most commonly played card too (not counting basic lands). Providing two colorless mana and only costing one, an early Sol Ring is unparalleled mana acceleration that can completely warp the course of any EDH game.

A colorless artifact, Sol Ring is playable in every single Commander deck, and unless you're deliberately trying to reduce the power of your deck, you should be using it too. If Sol Ring wasn't reprinted in every Commander product ever, it would be super expensive; as is, you can pick one up for a couple of dollars.

3. Craterhoof Behemoth

The best go-wide finisher

If you've played against any kind of green go-wide deck in Commander, and especially if you've faced an elves deck, you've probably seen a Craterhoof Behemoth. It's an ubiquitous win condition, that requires lots of green ramp (or green-mana hungry tutor effects) to put into play.

The Behemoth is a 5/5 green creature, with the keyword haste handily stapled on, that costs a colossal three green and five generic mana to cast. The stats aren't worth the cost, but its enter-the-battlefield ability is a game ender: all creatures you control gain trample and +X/+X until end of turn, where X is the number of creatures you control.

This increases the total amount of power on your side of the board by the number of creatures you control squared. It's an incredible pump effect, and because it's attached to a creature and not an Instant or Sorcery, you can find it using green's excellent tutor effects. Unless your opponents can counter the 'hoof, or deploy a board wipe or fog effect at instant speed, they're toast!

4. Gaea's Cradle

The best MTG land you can actually play

An land only needs to produce two mana when you tap it to be, objectively, broken. Gaea's Cradle produces one green mana for each creature you control. It's a terrible first land drop, but as long as you have a way to make creatures, it's the most broken mana-producing land in the game.

It's legal in Legacy, Vintage, and Commander, so this is a card you can realistically get to the table - providing you can afford to buy a copy. It's a reserved list card, that trades for hundreds or thousands of dollars depending on condition.

Tolarian Academy is arguably more powerful, producing one blue mana for each artifact you control, which are easier to generate and harder to kill. But it's only playable as a one-off in Vintage (and formats that follow the Vintage ban-list, like Canadian Highlander), so we're giving the spot to Gaea's Cradle.

5. The One Ring

The strongest artifact MTG card

The One Ring is probably best known for Post Malone spending $2 million to buy a limited edition printing of it, which is, admittedly, pretty exceptional. But it should be best known for being an absolute back breaker of a mid-range artifact in constructed formats.

For four mana, when the One Ring enters, you've got protection from everything for a turn, which pulls hard on aggro strategy's brakes. Then you can tap it, put a burden counter on it, and draw as many cards as it has burden counters. This is a ridiculous source of card advantage, and it's indestructible, so your opponent has very few ways to deal with it.

The One Ring's controller takes damage each upkeep from the burden counters, but who cares? It draws six cards in three turns. If you've got a Sheoldred the Apocalypse in play, you'll be gaining life. And since The One Ring is legendary, if you have multiple copies in your deck, you can cast a new One Ring and sacrifice the old one, resetting the counters.

The One Ring was printed directly into Modern, so it has never been legal in Standard or Pioneer. It has also been banned in Modern, because it was miserable to play against. But it's still a relevant card in Legacy, Vintage, and Commander.

6. Griselbrand

The best reanimation target

Griselbrand is everything you want in a reanimation target. A 7/7 flying demon with lifelink, he can wipe out an opponent in three turns on his own - but it's his activated ability that makes him a true reanimator all-star. For seven life, Griselbrand lets you draw seven cards, refilling your hand and probably causing you to discard cards at the end of your turn to put another reanimation target into your bin.

Griselbrand is banned in Commander and isn't legal in Pioneer. For those formats, look to Atraxa, Grand Unifier, who has vigilance and deathtouch on top of flying and lifelink, and an almost-as-powerful card draw effect. When she enters, you look at the top ten cards of your library, and for each card type put up to one card of that type into your hand (the rest of the cards being tucked to the bottom of your library).

7. Swords to Plowshares

The best removal spell

Printed in Magic's first ever set and still unbeaten, Swords to Plowshares costs just one white mana to exile a creature at instant speed. Sure, its controller gains life equal to its power, but that's a very small price to pay to ensure you don't lose the game - and one-mana instant speed removal for any target will stop you from losing the game.

The exile effect is important too, as it denies any 'on death' triggered abilities, and stops your opponent reanimating the creature later - very handy if said creature is Griselbrand…

8. Urza's Saga

The most value from a single land card

Urza's Saga is a one-card value engine for any deck that cares about artifacts. It's both a land and a saga enchantment; it offers you so much value that it's best to think of it as an enchantment that costs no mana, at the expense of skipping a land-drop for the turn.

The first stage of the saga lets it tap for colorless mana; the second stage lets you pay two mana and tap it to create a 0/0 colorless Construct artifact creature that gets +1/+1 for each artifact you control; and the third stage lets you search your library for a 0- or 1-mana artifact and put it directly into play.

Over three turns, you can hopefully generate one mana, create two Constructs, and tutor a Sol Ring, Shadowspear, or Skullclamp straight onto the board. In Vintage, you can even grab a Mox or Black Lotus; the fact that this tutors for those restricted artifacts means Urza's Saga is restricted in Vintage as well.

And, unlike the arguably more powerful Gaea's Cradle or Tolarian Academy, this isn't on the Reserved List - you may actually be able to buy a copy.

9. Lurrus of the Dream-Den

The strongest MTG mechanic

Our next entry is a creature which arguably got a whole mechanic nerfed - though there were certainly other problematic companions that helped it out. It's fair to say Wizards of the Coast dropped the ball with Companion, which lets you play with an eighth card in your hand, provided you meet restrictive deck-building requirements.

It definitely underestimated Lurrus of the Dream-Den, which could bring back permanents costing two or less from the graveyard. But luckily the downside, only being able to run permanents with a mana cost of two or lower, would dissuade most decks from using Lurrus, right? It's not like there's an archetype that relies on low-cost, low-to-the-ground creatures to win games swiftly, right?

While this cute nightmare made a big splash in Standard, it was even more deadly in eternal formats, where a higher caliber of one and two drops could be found. Lurrus is one of the few cards to be banned in Vintage, the most high-powered MTG format (there was no point Restricting it, since you only need one copy of the card in your deck).

After Wizards made the Companion mechanic far weaker, Lurrus was unbanned in Vintage. But even needing three mana to bring it to your hand, Lurrus was still too good for Modern, Pioneer, and Legacy, and ate a belated ban.

10. Pack Rat

The best MTG card in Limited

Pack Rat is one of, if not the biggest Limited bomb ever printed. This unassuming rodent, printed in Return to Ravnica, basically required an immediate answer, or it would multiply out of control, each copy making the rat horde, and the rats themselves, grow bigger and bigger. It didn't even matter what other cards were in your deck, if you could play an early Pack Rat and use its ability, the game was yours.

Umezawa's Jitte from Kamigawa also deserves a shoutout for making creature combat a nightmare. It also fit in any deck thanks to its colorless casting cost, but we chose Pack Rat for this slot because its apocalyptic approach to winning games is just so much more dramatic.

11. Oko Thief of Crowns

The best planeswalker card

Oko, Thief of Crowns has indeed stolen Jace the Mindsculptor's crown as the best MTG planeswalker. In true fey style, if you've never met this trickster before, you would not see the threat until it was far too late.

Oko's abilities are great, and highly versatile - being able to produce blockers and turn an opponent's impactful permanents into useless elks is fab. The real power comes in, though, when the abilities are combined with Oko's three-mana casting cost and loyalty values. He can be in play by turn two with a little ramp, and while the food token from his +2 ability isn't that impactful, he's then sitting at six loyalty - and dealing with him is an utter nightmare.

His controller can turn that food token into an elk to protect Oko, or shrink an opponent's threat into an elk. Oko's direct impact may not be flashy, but the opponent has to answer him - and all the time they're expending resources trying to remove the three-mana planeswalker, his controller can keep building up their own board, getting further and further ahead.

Fortunately, Oko is banned almost everywhere - he's not even playable in Legacy. If you get the option to grab him in a Legacy Cube draft, snap him up.

12. Contract From Below

Technically disqualified

Contract From Below is one of the best MTG cards ever printed. Just look at the value it provides. For just one black mana, you get a whole new hand of cards - that's absurd! Put four copies in your deck and mulligan until you find one of them.

The trouble is, of course, that you can only run Contract From Below if you're playing for ante, i.e. gambling with your cards. Ante cards are on the very short list of cards that are banned in Vintage (not to mention every other format). Perhaps there is a refined club of billionaires who exclusively play Magic as Richard Garfield intended - cards without set symbols, no sleeves, no card limits in deck construction - but other than that, this powerhouse is purely a collector's item.

13. Farewell

The best white board wipe

It slices. It dices. It makes you enemies every single time you cast it. Farewell is one of the most conclusive ways to reset a game, letting you exile any combination of all creatures, all artifacts, all enchantments, and all graveyards. It costs way more than the four mana benchmark set by Wrath of God, but its effects are so conclusive.

14. Tinker

The best MTG tutor card

Tinker does one better than the best tutors. It doesn't just fetch a card to your hand, it plonks an artifact of your choice right onto the battlefield.

Unfortunately, since the card's included in the Commander banlist, and isn't you're unlikely to experience the joy of trading a treasure for a Blightsteel Colossus - though you're allowed to run a single copy in Vintage, if you've got the cash.

15. Deathrite Shaman

The best mana dork MTG card

While Deathrite Shaman can't end games by swinging for damage, it's an incredible mana ramp card. As long as you're in a format where you can play Fetchlands to fuel your graveyard, it's essentially an upgraded Llanowar Elves that can heal you and damage your opponents without having to go through their creatures. Players jokingly call it Magic's first Planeswalker, since it's got three abilities and has such an outsized impact.

Unfortunately, the card has made its way onto the banlist for Legacy and Modern, the most accessible 60 card formats with those lands, and without them, Deathrite Shaman is a lot less funky. But it's an easy recommendation for any Commander deck running green and black.

16. Brainstorm

The best card draw spell

Brainstorm proves that you don't have to draw 50 cards to be the best card draw spell in Magic. In fact, while you get to look at three, after casting it you have the same number of cards in your hand as before.

Only playable in a select few formats, Brainstorm's strength lies in the sheer amount of card selection it gives you. While you have to put two cards back on top of your library, this isn't as much of a downside as you might think.

After all, in the first few turns of a Magic game you aren't casting every card in your hand. Brainstorm lets you stack the deck so you have exactly the cards you need, precisely when you need them. What's more, if you don't like the cards you put back on top, it's trivially easy to find an effect to shuffle way them away.

As a one-mana instant that replaces itself when you play it, Brainstorm fits naturally into decks that want to rapidly cycle through cards. It's handy for combo strategies, builds your Storm count, pumps Prowess creatures, puts an Instant into the graveyard to get you towards Delirium or enlarge a Tarmogoyf, and gets you closer to Threshold or pays for Delve costs…

And sometimes you would rather have cards on top of your deck than in your hand. Cast it on your opponent's end step to put a Miracle card on top of your library so it's your first draw of the turn and you can cast it for its Miracle cost; put a Crashing Footfalls on top of your library so that your Bloodbraid Elf will cascade into it; combine it with a set of Squadron Hawks and it's effectively a Time Walk.

It slices, it dices, and all for one mana!

17. Cyclonic Rift

The best (blue) board wipe

Though more recent cards like Toxic Deluge and Damn give Cyclonic Rift a run for its money, we say you still can't beat this classic busted boardwipe.

There are three factors to Cyclonic Rift's greatness. It can be a two-mana bounce spell if you really need it to be. It's one-sided, only bouncing your opponents' stuff. And you can play it at instant speed - you can hold up mana and cast this just before your turn, leaving your opponents with nothing to defend themselves.

True, Cyclonic Rift doesn't destroy anything - given a few turns, your foes will be able to rebuild and come at you with a vengeance. But if you play this card correctly, they won't ever have that chance.

Cyclonic Rift is the terror of EDH tables everywhere, to the point where it has a firm spot on the new-ish table of Gamechangers.

18. Mishra's Bauble

The best free spell (that isn't in the Power 9)

Mishra's Bauble is a very strange card. An artifact that costs no mana, you can tap it and sacrifice it to look at the top of target player's library, then draw a card at the start of the next upkeep. So you play it, gain a very tiny amount of game information, sacrifice it, and replace it in your hand at the start of your next draw step. What's the point?

In terms of direct impact on the game, Mishra's Bauble might as well not exist - and if you want to increase the consistency of your draws, that's perfect. It effectively shrinks your deck so that instead of running 60 cards, you can run 56 (with some little timing hiccups).

Indirectly, it's useful in a lot of other ways. It's an artifact, and plenty of cards care about artifacts entering, leaving, or being on the battlefield. It's trivially easy to get it into your graveyard: that puts an Artifact into the graveyard, handy for turning on a Dragon Rage Channeller's Delirium ability or pumping up a 'Goyf, and providing another card. And as it's free to put it in play, and free to put into your graveyard, it's absolute fodder for infinite loops.

Obviously it's no Mox or Black Lotus, but as we noted at the start, this list would be really boring if we just went through the Power Nine.

19. The Meathook Massacre

The best (black) board wipe

Black has access to a lot of great board wipes based on shrinking creatures' stats, which get around invulnerability protection, and Meathook Massacre is the best. This enchantment shrinks everything on the board when it enters, the exact amount depending on how much mana you pump into it. That flexibility is welcome - but it's the enchantment's triggered ability that makes it so potent.

Whenever a creature an opponent control dies, you gain one life; whenever a creature you control dies, each of your opponents lose one life. It's an aristrocrats payoff that was an absolute menace during its time in standard, and still a fantastic card in Commander.

20. Teferi's Protection

The best protection

If you want to keep your board away from harm, nothing does the job like Teferi's Protection. This spell not only keeps all your permanents safe, it also works as a fog until your next turn.

That's fantastic in multiplayer games like commander, and because the card is an instant, there's all sorts of ways to use it. You can pull a disappearing act in response to a boardwipe or attack, or use it on your own turn to prevent payback after overextending. There's no protection card as flexible and devastating as this one.

21. Esper Sentinel

The best one-drop

Magic has a lot of great one-drops, cards that will - if not win you the game on the spot - definitely set you up as the favorite. The best one-drop depends on your format, but in Commander it's hard to beat Esper Sentinel.

Ostensibly, white is the worst color at drawing cards, but then Wizards goes ahead and gives it this miniature Rhystic Study, which will ensure you stay ahead on card draw or keep your opponents behind the curve.

Like Rhystic, this card rewards teamwork and punishes selfishness. As soon as one player breaks ranks and refuses to pay their taxes, everyone else follows suit, leading to lots of lovely card draw for you.

And if you're seated at an unusually savvy table, you could always find a way to pump Esper Sentinels stats to make it even more back-breaking.

22. Orcish Bowmasters

The best hate bear

A diabolical card, Orcish Bowmasters is an allstar in all kinds of high-powered formats, because it punishes players for doing their favorite thing: drawing extra cards.

You can kiss one-toughness creatures goodbye when this guy's one the field. It's such a versatile card, it does removal, burn damage, and even creates bodies.

Though clearly born to be the villain, Orcish Bowmasters was the only defence Modern players had against the scourge of The One Ring (until that card got banned). The trouble was, most decks seemed to run both!

23. Blasphemous Act

The best red board wipe

Blasphemous Act is an example of a fun and fair Magic card, which nonetheless is extremely powerful. 13 damage will wipe away pretty much anything that's not worth targeting with spot removal, and the discount means you can often play this for just a couple of mana. There's a reason this card is in pretty much every single mono red commander deck.

24. Drannith Magistrate

The best STAX piece for EDH

If you want to make enemies on the more casual EDH tables, play STAX, a deck packed with hate pieces with the singular goal of stopping everyone else from playing Magic. If you want them to really hate you, play Drannith Magistrate - a two mana card that stops your opponent's from casting their Commanders.

It shuts down other effects as well - your opponents can't cast spells from anywhere other than their hands, so no casting spells using Madness, Plot, Mayhem, or a whole bunch of red impulse draw effects. But that's just extra poison on this particularly bitter pill. It's on the Game Changers list for a good reason!

25. An Untapped Island

The scariest card to face

Omg, what do they have?

How we chose the best MTG cards

There are dozens more MTG cards, from Griselbrand to Ragavan, that we could've considered for this list, and there's no scientific way to determine if one Magic card is greater than another. All MTG cards depend on the context in which they're played, the formats they're available in, and the other cards that help to make them sing.

To make our selections of the best MTG cards ever, we've tried to find cards that are dominant in multiple formats, or that would be dominant if they hadn't been banned. We've also tried to include cards you might actually run into or be able to purchase yourself, avoiding the most expensive MTG cards, stuff on the Reserved List that most players can't possibly afford. Obviously, that means the MTG Power 9 is out right away, which is good; that would've made this quite a boring list.

If you've got suggestions for the list, why not share them in the Wargamer Discord community? To keep up to date with all the latest news and features from Wargamer, make sure you're subscribed to the Wargamer newsletter.
excerpt: What are the best MTG cards ever made? There have been many, many Magic: The Gathering cards printed over the years, but most of them are destined to sit in dusty drawers, untouched and unloved. Not...

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: AIRCRAFT!
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m covering AIRCRAFT!

AIRCRAFT have seen one of the biggest shakes up of their rules in several editions with 11th edition. No longer zooming across the battlefield making impossibly tight turns, they now circle out battlefields, dipping in and out of the battlefield throughout the battle. This has required some fundamental changes to AIRCRAFT abilities such as how bombers work; let's get into it!

AIRCRAFT Set Up and Movement 23.01, 23.02

All AIRCRAFT in 11th edition must start the game in strategic reserves, meaning you’ll usually need to wait until round 2 onwards to deploy them unless your army has a rule or ability to circumvent that restriction. You cannot use the Rapid Ingress stratagem on AIRCRAFT; they are specifically excluded from the units it can target. Abilities that would allow an AIRCRAFT to deploy early include rules such as the Necrons Quantum Invader ability.

Quantum Invader: This model can be set up in the Reinforcements step of your first, second or third Movement phase, regardless of any mission rules.

When AIRCRAFT are deployed they need to make an Ingress Move.

AIRCRAFT do not generally have the FRAME keyword; this matters for Ingress Moves because it means it’s the base of the AIRCRAFT that needs to be wholly within 6” of a battlefield edge. Wings and extra bits like that can (and will) be further than 6” from the battlefield edge. Their wings and other parts are also allowed to overhang the battlefield edge without penalty; see later on in this guide for more context on extra large models.

Setting Up Large Models 03.02.02:

From Strategic Reserves…

Some large models, typically AIRCRAFT, have wings and other parts that extend significantly beyond their base. Such models can overhang a battlefield edge if it is not possible to set them up otherwise, but when setting them up, they must still be more than 8" away from all enemy units.

Once deployed they cannot move. All AIRCRAFT have been updated in 11th edition to have a movement of “-”. This value cannot be altered by any other rules.

Modifiers 02.02.01: Characteristics of ‘-’, ‘*’ and ‘N/A’ can never be modified.

AIRCRAFT too large to fit within 6” of a board edge

Some AIRCRAFT have very large bases, though. The Tigershark is on a 160mm base, for instance, which is 6.29”, making it impossible for such a model to be wholly within 6” of a battlefield edge without some slight geometric shenanigans. The corners of the board would allow the model to be wholly within 6” of two battlefield edges, some points being within 6” of one and some the other. This, whilst not specifically ruled against, actually isn’t necessary in 11th edition after an early update to the rules.

Setting Up Large Models 03.02.02:

From Strategic Reserves: If a model is so large that its base cannot physically be set up wholly within the distance required of the battlefield edge, it must be set up so that it is touching a battlefield edge. During a turn in which such a large model is set up on the battlefield (excluding AIRCRAFT models), that model’s unit cannot do any of the following:

    • normal/advance/fall-back/charge move.
    • Make any attacks with ranged weapons.

Normally extra large models are forced to enter the board and do nothing for a turn; AIRCRAFT are excluded from this.

Can AIRCRAFT deploy in terrain areas, or on upper floors?

There are no restrictions on placing AIRCRAFT models so that they are within terrain areas; if they fit with no parts sticking through and SOLID walls then that’s a valid position.

With regard to being deployed on upper floors, though, the answer is somewhere between yes and no. AIRCRAFT models do still have the FLY keyword which does allow a model to end a move on the upper floors of a terrain feature; however, to do so the model must fit its entire base on the surface of that floor without it overhanging. Very few terrain features will provide enough space to fit the typically large bases AIRCRAFT models use. So in practice, they can’t usually deploy on upper floors.

As such, the FLY keyword doesn’t do much for AIRCRAFT other than make them vulnerable to any ANTI-FLY abilities or weapons.

When do AIRCRAFT “move” again?

At the end of your opponent's next turn, you need to scoop all your AIRCRAFT back into Strategic reserves. They can then make an Ingress Move in your next movement phase.

Moving around AIRCRAFT in the Movement Phase.

This one is pretty simple: You can move through all AIRCRAFT models in the game. You still can’t end moves within another model or its base, and you can’t end a move within engagement range of enemy models. This does mean that they offer a limited amount of area denial whilst not specifically blocking movement itself.

Each time a unit makes any type of move, its models can be moved through AIRCRAFT models.

Though because AIRCRAFT must be deployed more than 8” away from enemy units when they arrive, only the fastest of enemy units would actually ever have a chance of moving through an AIRCRAFT with sufficient movement left to end that move outside of engagement range.

If you find yourself engaged with just AIRCRAFT models in the movement phase, your units don’t need to make Fall Back Moves.

Being engaged solely with one or more AIRCRAFT units does not prevent a unit from being eligible to make a normal or advance move.

Though after some talk around the TTB water cooler, it does seem like this rule is just trying to head off an unlikely scenario of being locked in combat with an AIRCRAFT. The chain of events that would lead this situation doesn’t seem like it will happen very often, requiring charges in or around an AIRCRAFT and some combination of Heroic Intervention and Consolidation Moves by models that can also FLY. Suffice to say, it’s not likely to be an every game occurrence, but better to have a rule on it now than not.

Making Surge Moves near AIRCRAFT

AIRCRAFT are also ignored when determining the closest enemy units for Surge Moves.

Each time a unit makes a pile-in, consolidation or surge move, unless that unit can FLY, while making that move, ignore AIRCRAFT units for the purposes of selecting enemy units and determining the closest enemy unit.

So you need to select the closest enenmy units that isn't an AIRCRAFT, it's not even a choice you're required to ignore them.

Shooting 23.02

There are a few exceptions to some key Shooting rules for AIRCRAFT in 11th edition, but there are just as many if not more that AIRCRAFT interact with in the same exact ways as everything else.

AIRCRAFT Plunging Fire

First things first: Because Plunging Fire might seem like it should apply to them, it does not.

The Plunging Fire rule (22.05) has no effect on attacks made by, or targeting, AIRCRAFT units.

I can certainly see why players would presume that AIRCRAFT get to benefit from the “I have the high ground” rule, but GW have decided to just exclude them from the rule generally rather than just when they’re the target.

AIRCRAFT Cover and Visibility

AIRCRAFT have no special interactions with the terrain rules in 11th edition. They interact with the obscuring and cover rules in the exact same way as every other model. Yes, this means that the Tigershark can gain cover from obscuring terrain areas.

This does mean that for many layouts, the amount of the board that will actually be visible to AIRCRAFT from the battlefield edges will be limited. If they survive the round though to re-enter in a later turn they will usually be able to find a target or two somewhere.

Remember that visibility checks are from any part of the model, not just its base. If you want more examples for visibility and cover please do check out my articles on Visibility and Line of Sight, and also my Terrain Guide.

Bomber Abilities

Now that AIRCRAFT don’t move, 11th edition has had to edit all of the Bomber abilities from the ground up. For now, at least, they tend to follow a similar pattern, but we might see more variation in them as the edition progresses and more Codexes are released. Here’s an example of one such ability.

Pulse Bombs: At the end of your opponent’s Fight phase, select one visible enemy unit (excluding Lone Operative units) within 24" of this unit, and roll six D6 for that unit: For each 4+, that unit suffers 1 mortal wound.

Pretty straight forward Mortal Wound generator. It is slightly odd that it excludes Lone Operative units from an ability that requires visible units, as Lone Operation in 11th edition does just cause units to be not visible to units more than 12” away.

Unless part of an attached unit, this unit is not visible to enemy models unless they are within 12" of this unit, and it cannot be targeted by [INDIRECT FIRE] weapons unless the attacking model is within 12" of this unit.

This is probably a result of the new Bomber abilities being written before 11th edition changed how Lone Operative worked by not letting units outside 12” target the unit, as it did in 10th, to 11th’s wording that makes the unit not visible.

AIRCRAFT in the Charge Phase 23.04

Being planes in the sky, AIRCRAFT have limited interactions with the Charge Phase. AIRCRAFT units are not eligible to declare charges themselves and can only make melee attacks that target FLYING units. How they interact with enemy movement in the Charge Phase, though, depends on the charging units' keywords.

Only FLYING units can select AIRCRAFT units as a charge target, and only FLYING models can make melee attacks that target AIRCRAFT units.

It’s important to note that even if you manage to get within engagement range of an AIRCRAFT unit with non-FLYING models, such as by charging another unit near the AIRCRAFT, those models still cannot target the AIRCRAFT. To target AIRCRAFT with melee attacks, the model attacking must have the FLY keyword.

Pile In and Consolidations Moves around AIRCRAFT

Whilst the exact wording of this rule is perhaps less than perfect, the intent seems pretty clear.

Each time a unit makes a pile-in, consolidation or surge move, unless that unit can FLY, while making that move, ignore AIRCRAFT units for the purposes of selecting enemy units and determining the closest enemy unit.

Unless your unit has the FLY keyword, simply ignore enemy AIRCRAFT when checking for Pile In targets, or when determining what type of Consolidation Move your unit will make and in what direction it will need to move.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!  Have any other questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
