title: [Warmachine] Summer Slaughter IGQ Retrospective
content:
Credit: Wolfe_The_Cat

Hello and welcome to another debrief of my time attempting to be a semi-competent competitive player of Warmachine! This week I’m talking about my recent excursion to the most awful place in the world for a pretty good two-day event. That's right, we’re talking about the Summer Slaughter held at The Crowne Plaza Princeton Conference center in… New Jersey. We’re gonna go over the venue, the preparation, the lists, the games, and a quick retrospective after the fact, so let's get right into it!

The Venue

Summer Slaughter is a multi game system event held by the fine folks at “Wicked Dicey.” I don't know a ton about the history and the internet has been less than helpful in that regard unfortunately. It did look like there was a decent turn out though between various GW games, Star wars Legion, Infinity, Halo: Flashpoint, Flesh and Blood, and of course Warmachine. The convention center (and future home to the Bokur Brawl) was attached to the hotel by means of a fairly long sky bridge, which made it very easy to get around and made the after tournament activities even easier, knowing you could have a drink and not worry about driving. We also had plenty of room between tables, in the rooms and within the venue itself, so you didn't have to be on top of anyone. The amenities were pretty nice, with lunch being available nearby and, while not outstanding, the food was good enough at relatively reasonable prices. The only real downside is the two conference rooms we were in did not appear to have working AC. This became a problem very quickly when the temps outside hit 90+ and the rooms all around us were full of people, effectively turning it into a swamp almost immediately. Not going to lie; it felt a little less than ideal. We were however told that we would be in different rooms come the Bokur Brawl next year and the AC did work in those rooms (we went up there to cool off a few times), so I have high hopes for how that is going to go and am looking forward to it!

Prep and Lists

Now onto the juicy stuff. Prep for this event was a little different than usual, what with Fane of Nyrro just coming into its own and looking at the caliber of player attending. There were only two people below a 450 rating on Longshanks out of 30 and while Longshanks player ratings don't mean much (seriously they don’t), I find they do give a decent idea of the general amount of games played and a vague notion of skill level. All that is to say the event was full of what I would consider mostly competent players; an excellent training ground for sure.

What this really meant for practice, though, was that the fundamentals of positioning and clock management would be key as no one was likely to make a big silly error, and so we could expect the games to go long and be solid. Going into any event, I have found it is important to set goals that are achievable and measurable. If you walk into every event planning to win, you’re going to be disappointed almost always. For this one I decided I wanted to learn my match-ups better (a thing you should be doing anyway) but was aiming to finish 4-1. I felt like that was achievable, given the competition, but not a foregone conclusion -- it was something to work towards that was infinitely doable.

I have been running Old Umbrey and loving them, but have found making a caster paradigm I'm happy with kinda hard. The army has a bit of an issue in that guns exist and largely aren't very fast outside of being able to yeet a warbeast or two very far, which means your options for dealing with that feels limited either to Morozov, or Galina and then whatever else you want to play. Out of the two of them, Morozov is far more consistent as an answer, which is why he’s in almost every pairing; he kinda has to be. Hopefully this gets addressed in January by a tweak to Azlanov or Yana but for now, it is what it is. So following the crowd I decided to bring a 4 heavy Galina list, and a Morozv list I mostly borrowed from Dan Riker with one minor change; mostly I swapped out Stryx for the Starved. My thought process was I could drop Galina into most things and be fine, while Morozov would be a bit more targeted to gun lines and maybe one or two other things depending on scenario.

The Tournament

Saturday comes around, and we get over to the conference rooms, the veritable Seth Cohen and Zosia VanMeter are running things. The judges give their normal pre-event spiel, the tables are set and labeled, and the pairings are up!

Round 1

Scenario: Trench Warfare

I get to go into the wonderful Erica Bevenour playing Grymkin. Erica and I have been friends for a while now and never gotten a chance to play in person, though there have been a few matches on Wartable, so I’m excited to get into it with her and it felt very much like she had the same thought. We were joking around and the shit talking began almost immediately. Genuinely I couldn’t have asked for a better start to the day and round 1 opponent. Scenario is Trench Warfare and Erica is running two identical lists with different casters, Old Witch and the Heretic. I opt to follow my strategy and play Galina; Wild Aggression Primeval should put the fear of Morrow in the house, and the extreme threat ranges coupled with the RFP and work heavies should give me a good chance. Erica to no surprise drops the Old Witch. We roll off and I choose to go first, knowing that picking up board space to hopefully bully out an Early Ill Omens is going to be essential when I still have the option to not have to commit super heavy to it.

Turn 1: Everything runs forward, Refuge goes onto my Spear Primeval, Wild Aggression goes to Stryx, and we get the Sword Primeval as many corpses as we can, then we get as far up the table as I can safely. Erica responds by putting the Slaughterhouse within 15 of Stryx and the Sword Primeval, and spreads out around a forest leading to her 50 objective, and popping shroud to give most of her army stealth.

Turn 2: I look at it and decide taking the House before it can do anything is a worthy goal especially without Ill Omens being involved. The totem pops forward to get -1 Arm on the house, Galina goes, feats, rushes the Primeval and shoots the House to get Bait the Line, I reposition back and realize that I’m not supposed to be camping 2. I was supposed to pop Blessing of the Gods, get an extra fury and swap Wild Aggression to the Sword Primeval to crit fish. Well…shoot. I messed that up, but I decide it's still probably worth going for even if my odds just went down because of my own stupidity.

The Primeval gets loaded up to five corpses and charges the House, boosting to hit the charge on the Sword, and surprisingly gets the crit...but that’s the only one it gets, and leaves the House alive on 18. Stryx follows up and manages to get it into the dirt, and has enough fury leftover to use its animus and sprint back to relative safety. The rest of my army positions and we try and push scenario as much as we can. Erica responds by having her Cage Raged kill my Sword Primeval and pushing left hard. The game grinds down from there and finishes after top of 6 with only 17 seconds left on my clock and 1:20 on Erica’s, with her taking scenario 13-10. A great game and a loss that I am honestly not upset about; we both made some mistakes but played as best as we could and had a hell of a time doing it.

Round 2

Scenario: Wolves at Our Heels

I get paired into a gentleman by the name of Elliot I had never met; very friendly guy who immediately struck up a rapport and reminded me why I love this community. Elliot was playing Kithguard running Craighorn and Grimtusk. I honestly did not know what to expect in this match; my experience with Kithguard is incredibly limited but I felt like I could mostly figure it out, and if not, then it would be a great learning game.

Elliot decides to drop Grimtusk, and I drop Galina. I win the roll off and decide going second is the best bet here. Wolves is a very live scenario and from what I know, Kithguard have a very live scenario game. I feel like if I can control the scoring tempo I will be OK.

Turn 1, the trolls run forward with Grimtusk getting Carnivore and taking position behind a big central forest. Treewalker feels like a little more nonsense when someone else is using it against you. Wild Aggression goes onto Stryx, Refuge to the Spear Primeval and I get corpses onto Jezhana. The hounds walk forward and Skrobala rolls max shots and picks up a Guard Tower, before repositioning back out of melee range, planning for a big push and feat next turn to try and get as far ahead on scenario as I can.

On turn 2, Elliot ambushes a Jungle Troll off the board edge and picks up one Liegeman Warden. Grimtusk uses Blessing of the Gods for an extra fury, positions on the left flank in a forest with Chameleon Animus up, and uses Soothing Song to make sure her beasts stay calm. She's camping five Fury and within 15 of my Sword Primeval and Stryx, and importantly, she has a Mistborn base to base behind her. Bottom of 2, I stare at Grimtusk 15” away from two heavies and think there's no way she is safe there, but she is def 19 and camping 5. I measure some things out and realize Jezhana is in range of the Mistborn behind her. I need a boosted 9, but if I get that, she's blinded and drops to def 15, making her much more killable. If it misses, Jezhana is still in a good spot for a feat turn, and I think I can score 4-5 this turn, have my entire army under feat, be safe from a counter assassination and follow through on the original plan. Really, there's no reason to not try it.

Jezhana goes and hits the boosted 9. Game on. Galina goes, and boosts two shots into Grimtusk to get Bait the Line, puts 7 damage on her and forces one transfer out. Stryx charges with Wild Aggression needing boosted 8s...and misses the charge and second initial. Not great. Thankfully he doesn’t miss another attack and leaves Grimtusk camping 1 fury on 4 boxes. The Primeval gets rush from the feral and charges with just the Sword in range. He hits the boosted 9 on the charge, forcing out her last transfer, then buys and boosts to hit with his second attack, hitting and Grimtusk toughs, before I buy my last attack and auto hit to kill her. I realize afterwards I never moved my totem forward for the -1 Arm aura, which would have helped tremendously (running the numbers after its a 90% to kill her if the blind hits). I then get a nice long break to go cool down.

Credit: Wolfe_The_Cat

Round 3

Scenario: High Stakes

After the nice break afforded by an early assassination, round 3 pairings go up and I get paired into another Jersey local, Cori, who is another wonderfully friendly gentlemen playing Necrofactorium, specifically Nekkane and Sepsira. I am not sure what he will drop but the assassination angles in both lists has me concerned, so I decide to drop Morozov. Cori drops Sepsira, wins the roll off, and decides to go second.

Forced Evolution goes on the Starved, and Fog of War goes up, while we take up table space and try to hold the middle and we position around each other. Top of 2 I move the Starved up to contest the middle 50. I figure with Forced Evolution and Star Crossed from Jezhana, he is going to be a bear for Mechanithralls to hit and there are a lot of them, mostly just positioned to score my side of the board. Cori does the same; he puts Last Word on a Sludge Thrall before moving them up the left to contest my 40, in a cheeky attempt to kill a bunch of my Liegemen with the explosion when I have to feat it; he goes up 2-1 bottom of 2.

Top of 3, Morozov feats and combo smites the Sludge Thrall away. I send the Starved and the Sword Primeval into the middle to clear it out with the Primeval contesting his 40, and clear my flag, scoring 3 and going up 4-2. Cori responds by flooding the middle, but Star Crossed is too much for the thralls and he leaves the Starved alive on 5 and doesn’t contest my flag, bringing the score 5-4.

On top of 4 there are a bunch of Thralls; clearing them is hard and dice are not helping, but since the Starved gets a bunch of corpses to heal and goes back up to 18 boxes or so, I contest and just focus on killing models, bringing the score 6-4. Bottom of 4, Cori is running out of models and just keeps jamming, using the feat to push me from his flag and some cheeky slams to get the hounds out of the picture. Score 6-5. Top of 5 I finally manage to clear out most of the fighting units, and with both heavies still alive in the middle manage to go up 8-5. Cori, out of front line pieces and mostly down to supports, does what he can but ultimately cannot clear and contest, and ends his turn with 1 second left scoring me 9-5 and getting the scenario win.

Credit: Wolfe_The_Cat

Round 4

Scenario: Two Fronts

After three rounds, a bunch of us go to dinner to celebrate Dan Riker's birthday and chat games for the day. I’m feeling good going into day 2 and when Sunday comes and pairings go up, I see I am playing into House Kallus piloted by Mr. Jimmy Livingston. Following the trend of everyone else I had the pleasure to play, Jimmy immediately starts cracking jokes. We talk about the day before while setting up and he wins the roll off opting to go second. He drops Hellyth and again I drop Galina, knowing dusk doesn’t love anything that makes things harder to hit and outside Hellyth feat turn its likely to be an issue.

Turn 1 is positioning and the usual shenanigans that come with it. Top of 2 I realize I can get a Sword Primeval onto the Void Engine and with Galina feat reposition it behind the House, so Imperitus will either have to swing over the obstruction making it Def 17 (15 with Hellyth feat) or be under Star Crossed from Jezhana, both of which just sound miserable for him and gets me a boostable gun and some very annoying solos out of the list. I decide to go for it; I flood the middle and feat, picking up the Void Engine and a few Soulless Guardians. The Chosen of the Witch sit on the left flank under feat and get the Set Defense command card to really discourage the Last Watch from even trying to come in. Jimmy cracks back with Imperitus and leaves the Primeval grievously wounded but alive on 4 boxes, but importantly without a way to clear the center flag. He scores 2 to my 1.

Top of 3, the Sword Primeval frenzies and misses his attack (sad trombone) but is still engaging Imperitus with Vorony keeping him securely stuck in place. Jezhana charges Imperitus, getting Starve on him, and I burn Careful Recon to back her into the Trench. My game plan at this point is to not commit into Imperitus unless I absolutely have to and just keep pushing scenario instead. My ambushing hunters swarm his 40 and I clear and score mine, my 50, and the flag, going up 4-2.

Imperitus kills the Primeval and Prisoner 102822 gets to live the dream, eating through four dudes before stopping in my backfield and the last of Lanyssa's Beasts back up to score the 50 on that side. He can't clear and score his 40, though, so the score goes 5-3. Galina starts backing out of the middle, knowing assassination is going to start looking more temping and making a point to get out of dodge. The Spear Primeval manages to hit the crit on Lanyssa's Beast and pushes it off scoring/contesting, letting me score the 50 side; the last Chosen of the Witch charges the Prisoner and doesn’t kill her, but does 4 boxes and blinds her. Bringing the score 9-3. Jimmy makes a valiant last stand but, low on clock, is only able to clear his 40 and contest before calling it a turn and giving me the win 9-4 on scenario.

Round 5

Scenario: Payload

Going into the final round at 3-1, I’m feeling good. Pairings drop and I see I get to play into the one and only JVM. Jake and I have played a few times over the years between various cons but with his dislike of the mirror he's always tried to dodge me when possible. This time, though, he can't dodge and we're both excited for what is sure to be a great game. To no surprise he drops Lylyth and again I drop Galina. I wish I could remember more of this game, but it was round 5 and intense. We both made some very silly errors early on and he capitalized on it better then I did, on top of both of us having a turn where boosted 8s were apparently a thing that was unheard of for our dice. We played it out to turn 7 where he took me on scenario 21-17, with him having two seconds left on clock and me having a little over a minute, and the only models left on the table being Lylyth, a Shadowmancer Scion, two Hydrix (one which was two-thirds dead), Galina, a Feral, the Totem and one of the Hounds. It was an absolute drag out slugfest that I learned a lot from and was glad to play.

Credit: Wolfe_The_Cat

The Aftermath

So after all is said and done, I finished the weekend 3-2 and 12th place overall. Goal not exactly accomplished, but both losses were close. Importantly, what did we learn? First, the clock training is working; aside from game one I was doing better then every person I played into on time. It made those later turns much easier and gave me a little more space to make sure I wasn’t making a mistake. Definitely a thing I think I’m going to continue doing for the foreseeable future. Second, knowing when to play an off list is important. I feel like my match into Dusk might have been a Morozov drop, and while things worked out this time it is absolutely a thing I need to learn more and make sure I’m dropping the right list into the right matches. Third, a highly mobile battle group is only as good as your positioning and fury management. Multiple games with the Galina list I had beasts taking frenzy checks turn over turn. You need to be able to manage the fury or plan for things to frenzy and be pleasantly surprised if they don’t, but you cant walk into every turn 2-4 FURY over, and think nothing bad is going to happen. Additionally I was positioning Stryx like he is any old heavy, and not taking advantage of flight and admonition as much as I can/should have.

Honestly great lessons to learn, a great experience and one I’m happy to have done, will likely do again. If you've made it this far, thanks for reading and see ya next time.

title: Commander Focus: Dwarves, Wheels, & Balin, Loremaster
content:
The history of Dwarves in Magic is a storied one. Receiving their first big typal push all the way back in Odyssey (funny name for a set in a world without Odysseus, in retrospect), it took all the way until Kaladesh 15 years later for the next evolution of the type. There, they were bound with Vehicles, which lasted until Kaldheim, where they were linked additionally with Equipment; to make a long story short, since Kaldheim, Dwarf typal support in some form has been around every year, ebbing and flowing with worlds in which the stout of body and large of heart were relevant. Middle Earth is of course one of those worlds, perhaps the world, and as we return to it in The Hobbit there’s no shortage of cards to excite Dwarf enjoyers. The thing is though, Dwarves already have a quintessential typal Commander, one that is arguably the best Monocolor Commander in cEDH, Magda, Brazen Outlaw. She isn’t really typal, if you actually look at her, but that doesn’t stop a deck at the format’s highest level of play from unironically jamming cards like Bloodfire Dwarf with intent to see it in the opening grip. Magda is typal, but only insofar as she cares that Dwarves…are, that they exist, and are cheap. That tradition continues with my favorite Dwarf from The Hobbit, Balin, Loremaster. While he’s slower than Magda, in Brackets a step below cEDH he’s arguably stickier, and merges Magda’s play patterns with that of another famous Red-adjacent cEDH darling, Etali, Primal Hunger. Let’s talk about how.

"If you have an enduring story..."

Let’s start with Balin’s condition, because it hinges upon a new mechanic from The Hobbit, the ‘Enduring Story’. Much like Ascend, if you ever control a card that mentions an Enduring Story, and you control 3+ historic permanents, you have that story marked as ‘on’ for the rest of the game. In Commander, given Balin himself is a Legend, and we probably have spare Treasure tokens or Legendary Lands lying around, this is functionally flavor text. It does matter a bit more in Limited, but I have a hunch it will be on for most decks anyways. Onto the meat of his textbox though, and we see that Balin affords you a wheel (for the same number of cards) when he or a Dwarf enters, pinging opponents for cards discarded if you have an Enduring Story. This is already fairly silly with anything that benefits from mass discard, like Surly Badgersaur & Magmakin Artillerist, but once you realize Dwarves have an abundance of exactly 1 mana Creatures you’ll realize this will often trigger 3-4 times per turn if untapped-with. These are essentially mana dorks in Magda, but here they’re Fateful Showdowns that hit each opponent; the floor is obviously a heck of a lot higher with the queen of the Dwarves, but Balin is his own form of insanity, albeit slower. Moreover, Balin works wonderfully with a second suite of cards you often see in Monored, which aren’t typically used in Magda: Temporary clones.

Turns out it was super easy, who knew?

Twinflame, Heat Shimmer, Molten Duplication, and more—these are where Balin actually gets his power. Unlike in Magda, who can make use of these 1-mana Dwarves from the first turn by coming down early, at 5 mana Balin requires a fair bit more setup. Just playing a 1 mana functional-vanilla feels pretty rough until he’s on the battlefield, so the density we play needs to be a tad austere. Clones though, they never go out of style. Of course they combo with Dualcaster Mage, but in Balin, they each represent 2 triggers of his ability on resolution, with the enters effect of the clone, and the original Balin seeing his mirrored copy, before it dies to the Legend Rule. While the damage is of course nice, and stacks up handsomely, the real power of Balin comes down to simply seeing enough cards. While you’re dunking opposing faces and ripping through your Library by way of cheap Dwarves & clones, you’ve probably pitched a considerable number of cards. Whether you intend to get them back with a Bag of Holding, or have cycled them to top each trigger via Library of Leng, Balin gives you the tools to continue his funny little game, so long as you play a necessary density of ways to both trigger him…and retain the necessary cards in hand.

Playing with Advantage

Red is very good at churning out mana, playing through hate, and putting a clock on your opponents. Those traits are not conducive to a large hand size, and Balin certainly feels that if built haphazardly. While you can pop off pretty fast, by way of rituals and means of pitching for mana, by the time Balin comes down it’s not unlikely you’re only wheeling for 3-4 cards, and that isn’t thrilling for the investment. Therefore, part of the challenge that Balin poses is squaring the circle of red card advantage in hand; impulse draw, its main means of seeing cards, won’t cut it here. Red traditionally lacks ways of filling their hand, outside of exactly Wheel of Fortune and its peers. Those cards are good, and in here, but if you’re entirely reliant on them be prepared to be disappointed. The good news is that you can use a hypergeometric calculator to get a rough idea of your likelihood to hit a card that propels Balin forwards, based on the number of cards seen. Essentially, if you plug in every Dwarf & temporary clone being played in your list as intended targets, you can then modify the sample size and pool size to get a feel for how many targets you need to play.

He will never be ballin'. He has always been Balin.

This gets even cooler when you realize a temporary clone provides two wheels (albeit, you’d need to cast at Instant-speed to use cards from the first redraw), so some number of your cards expand the sample when seen. For Flash Dwarves, we’re minimally-invested, with just Emergence Zone & Winding Canyons, but it does still come up. Just remember, unless your Dwarves are cantripping, every time you see a new sample it’s n-1 cards, where n is number of cards played from the hand. If you want your wheels to go positive on advantage, look to Phial of Galadriel, one of my favorite non-combo pieces to look for in the midgame. Whenever we're drawing cards via a wheel, Phial nets us an extra card, as we're emptyhanded before the new set of draws occur. The lifegain isn't just incidental either, because as we'll cover later, giving Balin Lifelink is unironically part of a win condition. If you’re just trying to pop off though, making your {R}-cost Dwarves free is the more important part, even compared to advantage. Birgi, God of Storytelling & the new The Vision and Scarlet Witch do this readily, but if you’re willing to get your hands dirty, a Phyrexian Altar is just as powerful. For whatever reason, storming off by gambling on finding Dwarves and shooting your opponents until you bust out is wildly Dwarven. Slam that comically-oversized keg on the table and roll those bones.

Stop Posting About [Baller]

You know now how Balin operates in a general sense, but what are the actual paths to victory? The most obvious is of course via DCM, Dualcaster Mage, which goes infinite with hasty bodies alongside any of Red’s clone spells. It’s a mainstay of the color identity, especially in cEDH/Bracket 4, and especially so for a list already excited to run those Twinflame-style clones. Why isn’t it in this list, then? DCM is my high water mark for what separates Bracket 3 & 4, being a reasonably-redundant 2-card combo that come down as soon as turn ~3, alongside rituals; it’s not as resilient for Monored as a combo like Underworld Breach+Wheel of Fortune+Lion’s Eye Diamond, but it certainly is faster—too fast, in my eyes, for where I’d want Balin to sit. Besides, we have significantly cooler ways to win here, starting with quite the novel concept for the color, in giving our Commander Lifelink. Balin can repeatedly deal chunks of 10-20 damage across three players, as we cycle through our Dwarves, and one of the best ways to use this excess life is via Treasonous Ogre, who in turn exchanges 3 life for a single {R}. With three opponents, that means a single discard with Lifelink generates one mana, and from there we’ve more than got the capabilities to tear through hands and find Dwarves, as we push towards the endgame. The biggest boon to this line is how accessible it is; Lifelink arrives via Witch’s Clinic, Hidden Hideout, & Shadowspear, with the former two being extremely low opportunity cost Lands we can incidentally find while we’re cycling hands, and the latter being a 1-mana Artifact, available via Urza’s Saga, Goblin Engineer, & Tezzeret, Cruel Captain. The Ogre, meanwhile, has the right power to be accessed via Imperial Recruiter, and can be utilized from the graveyard via Agatha’s Soul Cauldron & Dermotaxi (both of which can likewise be accessed via Engineer). Note that Hideout’s counter requirement can be filled by things like Agatha’s…or Dwarven Armorer. Not as free as other options, but it’s come up! You can put some iteration of this combo together about as frequently as the Breach line in Red, and that’s saying something, because wow is it sick to pull off.

Get to spinning.

One of the best ways to find more Dwarves to cycle Balin’s ability is via pieces of our other combo, Cloudstone Curio, two nonartifact 1-mana Dwarves, and a way to break even on mana. I say nonartifact because we are on Universal Automaton, and ~9 targets besides. There’s a caveat to that caveat, however, as with the inclusion of Fíli and Kíli, Joyous that number rises to 10; costing 3 and producing {R}{R} with haste, these are effectively the same cost as all our janky vanilla-ish Dwarves for combo purposes, albeit with a higher initial cost to kick off. In terms of ways to go mana-neutral, there’s Birgi, God of Storytelling, The Vision and Scarlet Witch, and the previous Treasonous Ogre line. In all these cases, we win via Balin damage. Just don’t forget to stack your triggers such that you discard before the Dwarf is bounced via Curio.

Example Decklist: Balin Out of Control

You’ll notice immediately that we’ve forgone fetchlands here, and that’s a purposeful choice; we’ll be ripping through our Library by way of Balin, and so in the mid-to-late game there’s a very real chance we won’t have the necessary basics to fetch, given the density of Legendary lands. Getting an Enduring Story isn’t difficult, but we never under any circumstances want to have a gamestate where it’s off when Balin comes down. Monored lacks the Landfall synergies, or use for cards in the graveyard, to really make fetches necessary, which is a benefit for those playing with a budget (and/or without proxies). Some Red decks definitely still want them (Tersa Lightshatter & Gau, Feral Youth are great examples I’ve covered before), but in general a deck drawing/milling a ton will get less value over time unless you’re on ~16+ basics.

While we’re not what I’d call a “traditional” typal strategy, there are still worthwhile tools available which hinge on the fact we’re full up on Dwarves. In my eyes, the biggest one is Heirloom Blade, which allows us to ensure there’s a Dwarf to continue Balin’s chain of triggers, so long as the wielder meets an untimely end. That can be achieved via Phyrexian Altar or Lazotep Quarry, though of course it also works as a rattlesnake effect to prevent attacks where we’d be able to block. Though there’s a chance we could in theory run out of Dwarves, the amount of wheeling that occurs makes it worthwhile to include one of the shuffle titans, if only to reset our Dwarf count in Library. Another typal piece of note is Mana Echoes, which produces an inordinate amount of Colorless mana; this is worse than if it were Red, as it prevents Echoes from slotting into our core combos, but the sheer amount of mana produced means the card still ends up being worthwhile.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

As is always the case with Monored, pushing the deck to B4 does mean you get access to Blood Moon, and thanks to Balin, you’re far more likely to see it or Magus of the Moon throughout the course of a given game. The truth of the matter is, however, that Blood Moon these days is only-okay. Rocks are plentiful enough that unless it’s coming down in the first three turns, most players won’t be stalled, and ergo Balin’s capacity to dig for it is moot. I believe Balin solidly sits as a great pick for high B3, with the opportunity to skew low if you lean more into Dwarf typal as the theme, rather than just an enabler.

Mogged by Magda

DZO contributed to one of the most striking showcase frames of Magic history, and Magda's is a fantastic part of that.

Magda is a tough act to follow, for Monored Dwarves, and frankly Monored as a whole. It’s an unglamorous thing to be compared to her, because she’s one of perhaps the best Commanders of all time. She’s in Vintage Cube, appears frequently in top cut, and is the second-most-popular Monored Commander on EDHREC. I remind you of this, dear reader, because absent these comparisons to Magda, Balin would be the coolest Monored Commander released since Final Fantasy, if not further beyond. If he didn’t mention Dwarf, and instead honed in on some modestly-supported type, I guarantee you there’d be ample praise to be had, but instead at 5 mana he’s trapped in the outlaw’s shadow. In spite of this, I’ve had an absolute blast with him as a Commander, and because he plays so differently to Magda—churning through options via wheels rather than tutoring key pieces directly—he suits my preferences & playstyle far more. Nothing gets me excited more, as a Johnny, than wresting control of variance from cruel mathematics, and seeing as many potential options as one can. The fact Balin kills your opponents while you’re busy rifling through your deck is just a bonus, really.

Until next time, forge an enduring story.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 34: Mailbag
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about switching to Grand Coven and running a practice game with my Thousand Sons against my friend T - which ended quickly when I got too aggressive. This time around I'm shifting to my plans for the 2026 Grand Narrative and the army I'm taking. I'm also going to talk about HeroQuest. But first, I'm going to answer some READER QUESTIONS. It's time for the first ever ROAD THROUGH MAILBAG.

These questions come directly from our Warhound Patrons, asked via Discord.

Nurgler: How the hell do you manage being a good dad and completing anything at all paintwise?

This is a good one to start with. And I'll set the record straight: I am, at best, an average dad. I try to engage with my son when he's home and steer him to make good decisions. I think the hardest part for me has just been engaging with him in ways he likes - one thing about kids is that for at least the first nine years of their lives they really want your attention all the time and will be happy with whatever you give them, provided there isn't a screen to look at instead. Once that thing goes on, you're dead to them.

So one thing I try to do is to find areas our interests overlap. It's not always going to happen - while I really like drawing and he likes drawing, my son doesn't really like sitting down with me and doing art. He really only ever wants to do art at school, specifically when he's not supposed to be doing it. So that one's out. And painting minis is tough - he was motivated a couple of years ago to get his marines painted for Armies on Parade but he's been pretty indifferent about it ever since.

On the other hand, we've had him learning to play drums in School of Rock for the past year or so, and as he's done that I've been able to help him practice by dusting off the guitar and playing with him. They do a lot of more modern songs, so when they pick something like "Big Me" by the Foo Fighters I can pick that up because it's a song I learned to play like, 30 years ago. And practicing with him gives him the kind of encouragement I didn't really have as a kid - while my father is a solid musician, he's never really had the patience for practice (I have no idea how he got good himself), or listening to me practice. When I was a kid he'd tell me to knock it off whenever I practiced trombone, partly because it was loud as hell and usually in a space near where he was watching TV. I'd eventually learn to play guitar, but that was by teaching myself in college.

Likewise, I'll sit down and play some games with him - just last night we decided to start on a big family playthrough of the original Final Fantasy VII - it's my wife's favorite game, and we're letting him take the reigns on the playthrough and just doing occasional voices for it. He has to read all of Cloud's dialog (he renamed Cloud to his own name, and named Barrett "Dad"). It's a fun family activity for us at the moment.

Then there's HeroQuest. We've been playing HeroQuest at least one weekend a month for like two years now, running through games of the main quest and First Light, alternating often between the two with some of my son's friends. I've loved HeroQuest forever and greedily picked up the Avalon Hill re-release and every expansion, plus a host of 3d printed accessories from Etsy over the years. I'm slowly painting all of it. Right now I've painted the entirety of the base set, most of the player characters (I still need to do the female dwarf and male elf), and a lot of the extra stuff from the deluxe edition of the original rerelease. I also finished painting this dragon before last weekend:

This past weekend we added a new player - another of my son's friends from school - and she took the Monk character as they battled their way through the final dungeon of First Light, defeating Qwindrak and freeing the baby dragon in the Seerscale egg. It was a cool moment, and our new player was hooked (we're already planning the next HeroQuest meetup). It's something he really enjoys doing and having the kids over to play has been great. I make them read every card and let them make mistakes.

I wrote about how to run HeroQuest with kids in this article.

This past weekend the missus was out of town so we set up the 3d printer. He's been asking me for things nonstop, and has shown an interest in painting them so they aren't just the same color as the black filament I put in the printer. That's been a fun experiment as well, and using it was easier than I expected. It's a Flashforge printer my mom got on sale a while back for my son, and it sat in my garage a long time before I finally took it out, assembled it, and started using it. It's easier than I expected but also just as pointless - unless you have something very specific to do with a 3D printer, they just kind of sit inert most of the time. So far I've printed a chaos emerald for him, the idol from Raiders of the Lost Ark, and I'm currently working on a time stone from Sonic CD. The boy likes Sonic.

Incredisteve: how often do you paint, for roughly how long?

It depends. At the very least, I paint every Saturday night. My friends and I have a weekly "hang out and paint" chat on a private Discord server. And every Saturday night starting around 7pm EDT, people start hopping on. It's not always the same people every week and I don't always paint when I'm on it, but it's a great motivator to sit down and paint something every single week. It's also just a good time. We have about 20 or so people who rotate in and out, though most weeks I'm in there along with Alice (RagnarokAngel), Jeremy (Curie), Norman, Joey (Crab-stuffed Mushrooms), and Craig (masterslowpoke), though a host of other folks are on there pretty regularly. When I hop on there I usually do so until I crash, so around 4-5 hours.

When I'm not doing Saturday night hobby hang-outs, my painting tends to focus on project-related tasks. I'm starting to ramp up now on my Emperor's Children for the Grand Narrative, which will mean adding two to three sessions per week until November, usually around 2-4 hours each. Then I'll crunch before the event.

Chris_from_IT: Less a question and more a request for more work in progress pics for the Emperor's Children

Hey, great timing! I started back up on these. Here's a guy I literally finished yesterday.

Mesa: You’re committed to Chaos. How did you get into that kind of thing? I would also enjoy Pro Painting Tips

It started with HeroQuest, where the Chaos Warriors were the coolest models in the entire box. I fell in love with those, and when Codex Chaos came out in 1996, I was hooked. You can read more about my love affair with Chaos in my Night Lords army showcase, one of my favorite articles I've written for this site.

I've had two imperial armies over the years as well - my White Panthers and my Deathwatch - but they don't hold the same place in my heart as the Chaos armies. As for pro painting tips, I've written most of what I know in my How to Paint Everything articles, but I'm working on an upcoming subscriber-only series on wining best overall/best painted soon.

Gerebell: What have you found the most important mindset shift or concept to grasp to play well in 11e compared to 10e? I know the basics of good play are the same, but what's the most significant change to compete that you've observed?

I don't really approach it much differently. I worry less about actions now, since I'm usually running Purge or Take and Hold. I treat cover differently - I tend to assume that if I'm not explicitly behind a wall, I'm going to get shot. That helps keep me from overextending into open spots on the map. Few moments in 40k feel as bad as when a unit you thought was safe is suddenly exposed by some angle you weren't expecting or because you misjudged a distance and now you're going to lose the unit and the game. You want to avoid those moments.

Otherwise, simply focus on being reactive and forcing your opponent to expose themselves or make the first move so you can get the drop on them. When I ran two units of Scarabs, the goal was always to have them drop in and kill something, never to just sit there. If my opponent had their own deep strikers, I'd always hold mine until after theirs came in.

SoylentRobot: how is it to transport your army around to these events, got any tips n tricks for making it manageable?

I talk a lot about transporting armies to events in this column. Usually I make decisions about what to bring based on what I can transport and how. I notably only use a regular citadel case for my armies, and if something doesn't fit in there, I don't bring it. I decided my Tacoma army based purely on what fit into a single, small Citadel case.

I will occasionally magnetize things to make it easier, but if I had something like a double or triple defiler list, it would probably just not be something I took with me to events requiring I fly. I also notably do not like to check bags when I travel - I hate spending more time at the destination airport - so I try to work out solutions which let me avoid doing so. This does mean I've packed socks and underwear in my minis case before.

Temporal: on average how many games do you play against a person before you're comfortable popping the question "hey I am Not A Murderer, come play at my house so only one of us has to go somewhere"

I'm usually pretty casual about having people over, in part because I'm not worried that the average person I meet will be a murderer, and you can just ask people to leave if they suck. I'm usually more concerned that they're just going to be shitty to play against, and even that's easy to mitigate. Or that they're chuds. Even living in Texas, I'm not so hard up for friends that I have to put up with shitty politics in order to enjoy my hobby. I can play those people at events; I don't have to have them in my house.

That said, I'll typically talk to someone a few times and play them once at the store before I invite them over, and there are some people I've known a while who are still only store-only folks, though that's just as often to be because they want to hang out in a store instead of coming over to my house as it is me not wanting to invite them over. I've definitely had certain people come over and not get an invite back, but that has never been because of how they acted in my house and was always about something that happened later at a store or an event. They were perfectly fine and respectable at my house.

The other thing is just getting a second opinion or reco from one of your existing friends or mutuals. I have people I trust, and if they tell me someone's on the level, then I have them over.

And I mean, that's an important aspect - when we're at my house, I'm in control. They are my guest. I'll provide food and drink and a sick place to play, but if they get out of line I can ask them to leave. If they're shitty at the game store, that's a public space and I have no right to kick them out. But I also don't have a big problem inviting someone over if they seem cool - if someone seems decent I'll gladly take a chance on them, and ideally we'll hang out and do something that isn't even Warhammer.

You don't want to end up like the supposed "casual" players who openly brag that they don't play against "pubbies" or the people at the game store. That's ultimately how the game dies; you want to help it grow and bring more people in. One of my best friends is Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson - and I invited him over during the pandemic to play a game fully masked without ever having met him in person. Those early "Road Through" articles are littered with his many losses. He's now a co-owner of Tabletop battles and we recently roomed together at the GW US Open in Dallas, where he won Best Overall for Kill Team and I won Best Painted for 40k. He's brought his wife over. They're lovely.

Final Thoughts

This was a fun one to write. I've always enjoyed answering questions about the site and my hobby, and I'll probably do this again when I have another relatively "down" week. For now it's back to the Emperor's Children grind, getting the army ready for the Grand Narrative, and prepping my Thousand Sons for Challenger's Cup in a few weeks.

See you next Thursday.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Marvel Crisis Protocol Affiliation Spotlight: Storm, Uncanny X-Men
content:
Right after the 2026 crisis rotation came into play, I won 3 competitive events with my Storm X-Men roster. A couple things had changed that really benefitted mutants:

  1. Source extracts make up for their lack of steals as Extract holders drop them every round.
  2. Most activations in this roster are some combination of Move > Move > Interact, which also works fine on Source extracts.
  3. The removal of really fighty crises such as M’Kraan & Mayor Fisk means I’m rarely forced into having to fight.

Things were feeling real good. Then the 2026 errata dropped…and my roster got a combination of 11 additional health. Now feels like the right time to shine a spotlight on X-Men Gold and, more specifically, what they’re benefitting from most in the new world of MCP.

Storm

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

The only thing that happened to Storm in the errata was gaining +1 health on both sides of her card.

For a character that mostly stands at the back, throwing Lightning Bolts at people outside of her Stealth (Goddess of Storms) range…having the ability to survive an attack and then double move to a point and throw a Size 2 character off with Tempest is fantastic.

I usually do this at the end of Round 2 or 3, meaning she’s now very unlikely to be Dazed and KO’d in the following round. 

I play her like a coiled spring. She stands at the back in safety until the perfect time to strike, then she rotates, flips some points and throws some characters.

I basically never use Ice Blizzard or Hurricane. The best way to spend power on Storm is with Tempest. If I have more than 3 power (or 4-5 power if I’m on pay to flips…as flipping Secures is Storm’s #1 win condition), so I also very rarely use Eye Of The Storm. I think people value that too highly. A 6 dice Lightning Bolt can definitely still whiff - and if that leaves Storm with not enough power to Tempest, that’s a disaster.

Iceman

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

The absolute sleeper hit that is Iceman got a huge glow up in the errata.

His entire gameplan is to deploy on a flank and dish out Slow & Stagger to the enemy team while the rest of your team rotates to the opposite flank with all the Extracts. His primary way of doing this is Cold Snap, a superpower that requires him to be alive after being hit from Range 2.

With the health bump up to 6 / 6, he is now a lot more likely to do that.

Iceman single handedly won me games with the above play pattern when he was on 5 / 5 health, so this is a huge change for him. I take him on basically any game that requires people to double move around the board.

Emma Frost

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

I wasn’t quite done celebrating the recent thematic glow up Emma Frost got to her kit before they went ahead and gave her more health! Now sitting at 7 / 7, Emma is even less of a model worth going after.

90% of the time she transforms to her diamond form where she has 5 - 5 - 4 defences and can reposition herself into cover and outside of Range 2 to benefit from the Storm leadership, making her even harder to take down.

Her Normal Form side offers a ton of tools that pick apart annoying meta tricks like Re-Roll bubbles, Heroes For Hire/Bodyguards & Clapbacks and the like thanks to Power Inhibition (not to mention this also turns off cards like Fall Back & Sacrifice).

Not to mention that she can pull off a clutch double move > double pay-to-flip while also potentially throwing a Size 3 to end the game while in Diamond Form thanks to her 5 - 5 defences.

Emma Frost is great in any X-Men roster because she’s just plain good. She also brings an X-Men specific Team Tactics Card in the form of Headmistress which brings even more movement tech which they love.

Beast

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Beast didn’t get a single thing in the errata this year - and I’m absolutely fine with that. You can see some of my thoughts on Beast in the X-Men Starter Set write-up here.

He was a top tier model before the errata and he remains a top tier model now. There’s a bit of discourse in the online MCP community that Beast is now unplayable because of not getting any additional health? Well I’m here to tell you that is categorically incorrect.

Nobody's damage output was increased in the errata, meaning Beast is still as tanky as ever. He’s just surrounded by X-Men that now also have a chance to survive attacks, meaning his job of move > move > throw a character is still some of the best value in the game.

Gambit

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Gambit is great. Wilds counting as 2 thanks to The Cards Always Be In My Favor can make him a little unpredictable defensively, but it brings his ceiling up into the stratosphere when he does roll those sweet Wilds.

A Little Something Extra makes his attacks way more predictable, meaning he can reliably displace a Size 3 character with Bo Staff or ping some damage onto a character that survived on 1 by using Kinetic Ace on a target within Range 2 of them.

All of this paired with Enhanced Agility which is not once per turn and is not towards the attacker makes Gambit one of my most versatile and reactive models to play.

He got +1 health on his injured side in the errata, which mostly opens up more opportunities for a double 52 Card Pickup turn to turn the game in my favour when needed.

Angel

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Well…I never thought I’d see the day where I include Angel in a write-up like this.

It’s still early days for me to be trying him out on the table, but moving to 6 / 6 health means he doesn’t instantly get deleted from the game anymore. But he is still 3 - 3 - 3 defences, so it can certainly happen.

His kit feels super awkward. Most of his activations you want him to double move and pull off an Air Lift and a Hostile Takeover. He can’t be paired with Beast because that guy is too big to be air lifted apparently. He needs to start his move action within Range 2 of the people he’s trying to move around, which plays a lot more awkward than it reads.

In short, I’m trying Warren Worthington III out here. Another medium base for using the Storm leadership doesn’t hurt. Healing Factor is cute but he tends to take more damage than he can heal off.

I bring Ultimate Sacrifice because I can see that being pretty game winning if timed literally perfectly (he has to pay for it, then you want him to Daze to get the effect). Awkward awkward awkward is the vibe I get from this guy.

I think he belongs in the roster for sure, because a guaranteed Size 3 throw on Avenging Angel is no joke in later rounds when you have a scary Dracula or Mephisto stomping towards you. But I need more play time with him for sure.

X-23

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

This one breaks my heart, but I’m currently experimenting with taking X-23 out of my Storm roster. In a world where everybody and their mom got more health, X-23 stayed where she is. Which is fine, she was already a top tier model (you can read all about my love for her here). But 5 health means she can easily have her activation removed by other models.

She’s now also trying to take out characters with more health than before. Which she can certainly do reliably…just a bit less reliably than before.

If Angel doesn’t make the cut after my experimentation, it’ll be Laura who takes his place for sure.

Valkyrie & Elendil

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

I’ve been really loving Valkyrie & Elendil under Storm X-Men. 

On the surface, she offers a large base for using the leadership with and acts as a model that can chase Extract holders around the board more effectively than the rest of my roster.

But if you look closer at their kit, this deadly duo bring a lot more to the table. 

Take Wing lets them trigger the extra dice on Geirr without the need of a Storm leadership hop. 

Need A Lift helps get X-tract holders (see what I did there?!) out of harm's way while Valkyrie & Elendil rotates.

Guardian of Valhalla works really well in a roster full of X-Men that have a tendency to Daze, meaning my usual play pattern with Valkyrie is to chase down an Extract, run away to safety and slowly heal up over the rest of the game while the rest of the X-Men are dazing.

Speaking of healing, these 2 went up to 7 / 7 health in the errata which is a big deal as it gives them more chance to survive and benefit from Guardian of Valhalla.

Another use I love having Valkyrie & Elendil for is playing as goalkeeper. Once the X-Men are loaded up on Extracts and running away from the enemy team, Valkyrie can jump in and hit some people with Fury Of The Valkryor with a pretty reliable stagger, making it harder for them to chase down your VPs.

There are likely better models for this spot in the roster such as Omega Sentinel & Prowler. But I’ve had a ton of fun playing Valkyrie as she’s just a big old toolbox filled with utility. Plus she’s easily the best model sculpt they’ve added to the game!

Toad

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

A lot of people are down on Toad now that he only has 4 health and cannot displace enemy models. I agree with that; I can see him being a liability in most teams these days.

However, I now consider him to have passed his entry exams at Xavier’s School For Gifted Youngsters making him an X-Men affiliated character (in my head cannon only…he’s still only affiliated to Brotherhood of Mutants and Servants of the Apocalypse).

The main reasoning here is;

  1. He’s still good on pay-to-flips, which Uncanny X-Men use a lot of.
  2. He can use Finders Keepers to take an Extract off Valkyrie & Elendil or Angel, allowing them to dive towards the enemy team and get on with their usual jobs.
  3. Once Toad is holding an Extract, if he survives an attack and can use Slippery, you’ll likely never see him again and he’ll reliably score that VP for a couple more rounds. This makes him a prime target for Xavier’s Dream.

My opponent often laughs when I choose to save Toad with this card, but my whole gameplan is to reach 16 VPs before we ever see Round 4. Keeping Toad alive while holding an Extract long enough is a key part of that, so I’m never sad to have to do that if it puts a Slippery online (remember that he has to suffer some damage to trigger this, so don’t Xavier Dream too hard).

Cable

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Cable got more health in the errata. I don’t think he needed it. His best defence is killing everyone around him, which he’s great at.

More details on my thoughts on how to play Cable here.

Characters to Consider

Here is a list of characters that aren’t in my roster, but I am absolutely considering bringing in.

Gwenom

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

I played Gwenom at the World Team Championship in 2025 and bloody loved it.

With a Storm hop from the leadership, she can attack twice and move twice when using Symbiote Spider Technique.

She got additional health in the errata making the healing available from Maximum Gwenom a lot more likely to be useful.

She has Size 3 character replacement with Dark Rage, something X-Men sorely miss.

Pick On Someone Your Own Size is also cute as she’ll likely be surrounded by X-Men holding Extracts, so she can punish your opponent for having a swipe at them.

She’s very dice reliant as she really needs power to get her kit to go off. But with more health, she’s certainly likely to have an easier time generating it.

Wolverine

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Wolverine got a lovely subtle glow up in the errata moving to a whopping 8 health. 

You can read about some of the tricks this opens up here.

Nightcrawler

Image courtesy of Atomic Mass Games

Kurt’s job is generally to wait until the end of a round and then BAMF! & Puff Of Smoke around flipping points and hopefully stunning people.

Him moving to 7 / 7 health makes this easier to pull off as he won’t have his activation removed as easily as it used to be previously.

His spender is a lot of fun and tends to be what people talk about with him. I find it a little unreliable for my playstyle (I prefer guaranteed triggers / less painful gambles where possible), so I personally think the moving/placing around to flip points at the end of the round is a better play pattern for Nightcrawler.

Crisis Cards

In terms of Crisis Cards, I currently take:

Extract Crisis

Mutant Extremists Target U.S. Senators! (19)

Skrulls Infiltrate World Leadership (20)

Unexpected Guests Crash Royal Wedding (17)

Scientific Samples Found in Discovered Universe (17)

Salvaged Supplies Fuel Resistance Efforts (18)

Secure Crisis

Mutant Madman Turns City Into Lethal Amusement Park (18)

Guardians Save Shi‘ar Empress in Style (17)

Strike Team Secures Shield Relay! (17)

X-Men Infiltrate Secret Weapons Facility (17)

Power Overload! Factory Goes Up in Flames (19)

The main thing to note here is that I’m taking every pay-to-flip that I can, besides Deadly Meteors because it’s too close and despite the additional health, Storm X-Men still really don’t want to fight if they can help it.

There is some Round 1 jank you can pull off with priority, Emma Frost & Headmistress on Salvaged Supplies that is a few too many hoops to jump through to make it reliable. So I’ll likely take this crisis out eventually in favour for something like Inhumans Deploy Advanced Weaponry or Spider-Infected Invade Manhattan.

At the start of this article I mentioned that Uncanny X-Men are good on Source Extracts. I do believe this, but I don’t think they’re high scoring enough to include in my roster. I may be wrong about this, but I’ve just found Source Extracts are fine for us…not necessarily great enough to include them in the roster.

I also bring Power Overload! Factory Goes Up in Flames because with the inclusion of Angel & Emma Frost, I now feel like I have some answers to the Kingpin Criminal Syndicate types of roster that you may encounter here.

Final Thoughts

I’ve had a ton of fun playing with Storm Uncanny X-Men these past few months - and have been surprised at the success I’ve had with it!

With the additional health to almost the entire X-Men roster in this update (finally confirming my propaganda of AMG standing for Anti-Mutant-Gang was actually just straight FACTS), now is a great time to pick up some mutants and try them on the table.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Hanami board game review: A flawlessly sharp euro that's sweet as saké
content:
Our Verdict

Reiner Knizia's classic Samurai has been reimagined as a clash of picnickers, but it's no less striking for its re-theme. In fact, the new skin is gorgeous and thematically rich (though it doesn't always map perfectly onto the old mechanics). The core game may be almost 30, but it's still a seamless strategy experience that's as deep as it is accessible.

Pros
  • Seamless strategy
  • Approachable yet deep
  • Gorgeous production
  • Plenty replayable
Cons
  • Occasional thematic mismatch

These days, the word 'eurogame' comes with baggage. We expect elaborate table spreads, ten-year turns, and strategic web that gives even seasoned tacticians analysis paralysis. Hanami honors that last part of the genre's tradition, but it strips away the rest of the chaff. This is the kind of board game that makes reviewers say high-brow words like elegant. There's not a scrap of wasted space.

This won't shock anyone that knows Hanami's history. The accessible strategy game is a remake of Samurai, a popular game created by Dr. Reiner Knizia in 1998. Knizia's name is inseparable from the world of board games. He's designed over 800 of the things, and many of his works are considered the best board games in history.

Samurai is among the better-loved Knizia titles, so it's no surprise publisher Keymaster Games saw value in reviving it. Hanami will feel very familiar to Samurai fans, though Keymaster has added new action tiles, new ability cards, and an entire second map to the area majority game.

It also completely changed the theme. No longer are you Samurai bands vying for the favor of local factions. Now, you're picnickers competing for the best spot in the park, where you can eat bento and enjoy the blooming of Japan's famous cherry blossoms.

I adore the concept. Repositioning tourism as a battle for area control sends a stark message about how, in today's world, we commodify our experience of the natural world. Everyone wants the holiday snaps no one else has, and they're willing to fight to get it. Once tranquil natural scenes become crowded by experience-seekers (who usually see the whole thing through a second pair of eyes, their smartphone). There's so much desperation to collect these special moments that we forget to live them.

Japan has seen its yearly visitors grow from 10 million to 30 million in just ten years. Complaints of crowding and bad manners are rampant. One two even canceled its yearly cherry-blossom viewing festival this year because of tourists (Hanami, by the way, is the tradition of viewing beautiful flowers like the cherry-blossom). Japan is far from the only nation suffering from overtourism, but it makes a fitting site for a board game exploring the topic.

While the broader concept hits home, the theme sadly doesn't always map onto Knizia's mechanics. That's because these panicked picnics imply a vicious struggle for space. This is present in Hanami, but its bite is lessened by the game's symbiotic player relationships.

Let me explain. Each player has a pool of tiles they'll draw from to create their hand, and they'll place (at minimum) one of these tiles per turn. The goal is to place your pieces around parks on the board, where cherry blossom, lantern, or bento tokens are waiting.

When a park's land tiles are completely filled, these tokens are given to the player who placed the most valuable tiles in that 'suit'. Drop a four-pip cherry blossom tile, and you're a shoe-in to grab the related token.

Other players may scupper your plans, however, with wild tiles that count towards all token types. They might also throw in a special tile, which allows them to do things like sub in another tile of their choice that's already on the board, or copy the value of an adjacent tile. Plus, everyone has a powerful once-per-game ability card that can shuffle things even more dramatically.

You can learn to play Hanami in ten minutes, and even full four-player games won't last more than an hour (at least, not without some serious analysis paralysis). But calling it 'simple' undersells the wealth of decisions you have to make. Each tile placed is an opportunity lost or gained.

Much of this is down to Hanami's unique scoring system. There are only ever three points to claim, and they go to the person who collects the most tokens of a particular type. Ties are decided by the number of tokens in other suits you collected.

This gives you several things to juggle at once. You need to establish dominance in a suit, but you need to block others from doing the same. You also need a healthy backup stock of tiles for tie-breaks. Do you play your most powerful tile now, or save it for when you have a clearer idea of who your main rival is? Do you corner a token with fewer surrounding spaces now or wait? So many questions!

The special thing about this gameplay loop is that players need each other. Hanami's two boards are delightfully cramped, so every tile placed also helps your opponents further their goals. It's tough to surround a park by yourself, so you're often relying on the plays (or misplays) of others to score big.

Here lies Hanami's delicious tension. Here also lies that unfortunate mismatch in theme. If I stretch my imagination, I can see a more hopeful version of the game, where citizens work together to create a wonderful cherry blossom viewing festival (while also sneakily saving the best picnic spots for themselves). It's a less seamless ludonarrative, however, and a less impactful one.

This is my only fault with Hanami, however. It's hard to find any other flaw in Knizia's airtight design. The new additions by Keymaster only add to the game's replayability - giving this $40 board game (or $70, if you want deluxe components) tremendous value for money. If the core game wasn't already almost 30, I'd be hailing its innovations. All I can say is, if this Knizia classic has previously passed you by, Hanami is a must-play. Short, sharp, and sweet, like well-crafted saké.

Want to talk more about this year's big-hitting board games? Feel free to pick my brain in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of Hanami was provided by the publisher.

title: MTG Arena codes for August 2026
content:
MTG Arena codes are an essential, mostly free kick-start for your digital collection, unlocking new Magic: The Gathering cards, booster packs, XP, and cosmetic items like card sleeves, avatars, and more. Read on to find all working MTGA codes in 2026, as well as full instructions on how to redeem promo codes on PC and mobile.

Each month, as the MTG release schedule rolls on, we trawl Wizards' announcements about new MTG sets to update this list, telling you which codes currently work; which have expired; and which brand-new codes have sprung up for the game. The good news is that you can still unlock free cards to boost your MTG Arena decks.

Here's how to get MTGA codes:

  • All free MTG Arena codes in August 2026
  • Unlock the cabbage companion
  • MTG Arena rewards
  • How to redeem MTG Arena codes
  • Where to find more MTGA codes
  • All expired MTGA codes

All free MTG Arena codes in August 2026

For the first time in ages, and lasting until August 27, there actually are MTG Arena codes to be used! A chain of riddles, released alongside the Hobbit set, will win you some cards, card styles and a unique avatar. Here's what to do:

Right now, if you check your inbox, you'll find a riddle. Input the answer as an MTG Arena code in the store to unlock a reward and the next riddle. Keep going until you've answered all eight, then create a deck with all eight of the cards you just unlocked. 

It doesn't have to be legal, or even have the correct number of cards, so just plonk them all in and save it. Name the deck 'Riddles in the Dark', and you'll receive a Bilbo avatar.

If you want to try to solve the riddles yourself, exit this page right now. We're assuming you're here for the answers, which you'll find below.

  • Riddle #1: Mountain (The Mountain-king's Return card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #2: Teeth (Gnashing of Teeth card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #3: Wind (Velvetwing Butterflies card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #4: Darkness (Gathering of Darkness card and borderless card style)

Can't find the cart? It's at the top of the battlefield, just to the left of your opponent's profile picture.

Is the cabbage companion better than the beachball or the pet rock? That's for you to judge.

MTG Arena rewards

These days, Wizards hands out free booster packs as MTG Arena rewards to celebrate the release of new sets. These arrive directly in your in-game inbox without the need to redeem a code. Plus, new players who complete the how to play tutorial are greeted with a whole stack of reward packs to crack open from the last couple of years' worth of sets (plus a selection of variant land cards to use).

How to redeem MTG Arena codes

There are two ways to redeem MTG Arena codes on PC, and both are dead easy - just pick your method below and follow our step-by-step guide.

How to redeem codes in the Arena client

The most common and simplest way to cash in your codes is directly inside the MTG Arena client. Here's how to do it:

1. Open up the game on PC and click on the 'Store' tab at the top of the page.

2. You'll see a small oval text box in the top right corner, with 'Redeem Code' written inside (we've highlighted it in red in the picture above).

3. Copy your code into the box and hit enter.

4. Your reward automatically appears in your account!

How to redeem codes via your Wizards account

If you'd rather not boot up the game, you can also redeem codes by entering them into your Wizards of the Coast account page. Here's how you do this:

1. Log in using your MTG Arena details, and on the right-hand side of your account dashboard, you'll find a nice, big 'Redeem a code' box.

2. Paste the code inside and click 'Redeem'.

3. The goods will appear in your account next time you log in to the Arena game client.

How to redeem MTGA codes on mobile

If you're primarily a mobile MTGA player and want to redeem codes on your phone, the process can feel a bit more convoluted, because - frustratingly - there's still no way to redeem codes directly through the iOS and Android versions of the game.

The main way to get the job done is simply via mobile web, with the following steps:

  1. Log in to your Wizards account via your mobile browser.
  2. Scroll down to the 'Redeem a Code' box as shown in the image above.
  3. Enter your code, and click 'Redeem'.
  4. Your rewards will show up next time you log into the game.

If everything's worked correctly, you'll see a little green message pop up that reads "Code redeemed successfully", as seen above.

However, if you really want to make things difficult for yourself, you can access that same account-based process from within the MTG Arena mobile client. We don't recommend it, though, because it's janky as all hell - it's far easier just to hop over to your mobile browser and do it there.

Where to find more MTGA codes

If you've already used all the free codes available, and still want to expand your collection of planeswalkers, creatures, and fancy land cosmetics, there are a few other places where you can sometimes get your hands on more MTGA codes to redeem. You can do this either by buying select Magic products that include Arena freebies, or else staying alert for new promo codes and other fans' unused codes shared online.

The main options to try are:

  • Physical Magic: The Gathering products
  • Social media giveaways and competitions
  • Promo codes from local game stores
  • MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

Physical Magic: The Gathering products

Unlike the Pokémon TCG, not every sealed pack of Magic cards comes with a digital unlock code included - but some physical MTG products do give you a code into the bargain, to grow your digital collection as well as your cardboard mountain. There are three types of products you can buy for this.

Prerelease kits

Wizards of the Coast launches each new Magic: The Gathering set with a pre-release event focused on in-person games in local game stores, selling Prerelease kits of six brand new boosters.

Since 2025, these prerelease kits have no longer included MTG Arena codes packed in the box. Instead, you'll register your Arena account when you attend the pre-release event at a physical store, and your free boosters will appear in your account when you next log in.

However, older prerelease kits can still be found for sale which do contain Arena codes. If you buy one of the following recent Prerelease kits, you can use the included code to unlock MTG Arena boosters for the corresponding set:

Product Reward Approx. Price Link
Murders at Karlov Manor Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon
Lost Caverns of Ixalan Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon

Starter kits

Starter kits are designed to get newbies into Magic: The Gathering, so they offer up two pre-constructed decks. The kits also come with a code that unlocks each deck in MTG Arena, too.

Buying a second-hand starter kit might mean that your code has already been used, but if you can get one new (or from a reputable, code-selling source), these are the decks to look out for:

Planeswalker decks

All physical Planeswalker decks released between the October 2018 set Guilds of Ravnica and Core Set 2021 came with a one-time code to unlock their cards in MTG Arena, so you could use all the same cards online.

Sadly, the older codes from these decks have now expired, and the decks themselves are very difficult to come by (they're all unavailable on Amazon US and UK) - so you'll struggle to find an unopened copy with an intact code for a reasonable price. Even more sadly, free codes isn't a trend that was carried on by the far more available Commander precons.

If you really want the physical cards too, though, it might be worth the hunt; here's the full list of decks with (we think) still functioning codes:

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes are found in Wizards of the Coast's limited edition, premium Secret Lair boxed sets of one-off collectible cards. The rewards vary, but usually, they unlock exclusive cards and cosmetics.

You can get some pretty sweet, limited edition skins, though - for example, if you bought the 'Warhammer Bundle' during the October 2023 Warhammer 40k Secret Lair, you got two codes, each good for ten premium card sleeves showing the 40k-ified versions of classic cards:

Beware, though - this is often the priciest way to find new codes. Each Secret Lair 'drop' can cost anything from $20 to several hundred bucks. We only recommend going this way if you really want the physical cards your codes will come bundled with.

Social media giveaways and competitions

If you're a social media-savvy Magic fan, another way to nab a cheeky extra code is through giveaways or competitions run by major MTG content creators, influencers, or simply kind-hearted fans sharing codes they don't need or want for themselves.

MTGA Codes, a retail website that collects unwanted and unused Arena codes and sells them directly online, regularly runs such giveaways to drive engagement on its Twitter account (@MTGA_CODES).

There's no way to know when such giveaways will take place, or exactly who's going to be doing them - but we can recommend a few creators you should follow just for regular, great content and commentary on Magic and Arena, who have been known to give away MTGA codes in the past:

  • Grzegorz 'Urlich' Kowalski (@urlichmtg) - former Magic Pro League player, Twitch streamer
  • Gerry Thompson (@G3RRYT) - Magic pro player from the US
  • The Asian Avenger (@Theasianavenger) - Magic YouTuber and streamer
  • MTGNerdGirl (@MTGNerdGirl) - Magic YouTuber and streamer

Promo codes from local game stores

It's not all the time, but Wizards of the Coast occasionally creates special MTG Arena codes as part of promoting in-person Magic play through bricks-and-mortar local game stores (LGS). Most recently, it did this via its 'Friday Night Magic At Home' campaign, aimed at helping stores keep regular play events going during Covid lockdowns in 2020.

This isn't a regular occurrence, though, and it's entirely dependent on Wizards' ongoing strategy for working with game stores - if you're angling for extra codes, we'd recommend checking in with the staff at your LGS to see if there's anything on offer.

MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

In the past, Wizards of the Coast has collaborated with other big brands to offer MTG Arena promo codes as a bonus for their subscribers - and, back in 2019, it gave away free unlock codes as a benefit for the Twitch Prime service (now merged with Amazon Prime Gaming).

All you had to do to get the code was sign into your Twitch Prime account, check the 'Loot' section, click on 'claim', and it would generate a code for you to redeem directly in the Arena client.

Sadly, we haven't seen any more new MTGA codes come through this service in the years since - but there's always a chance, so if you're constantly on the hunt for fresh codes, it's worth periodically checking in on your Prime Gaming account (there's also a bunch of free videogame downloads and other goodies there, of course).

Naturally, we'll also update this guide the moment we see any new MTG Arena unlockables pop up on the platform.

From February 2024 to February 2025, MTG Arena players could use a specific method to claim a free unique cosmetic and XP bonus. Wizards gave the freebies away as the reward for an ARG hidden in various products and marketing for the Murders at Karlov Manor set.

Code Reward Expiration date
thewayisopen (see Karlov Manor code instructions above) 5,000 XP and MKM card sleeves February 6, 2025

Sadly, the promotion ended on Thursday, February 6, 2025 - so you can no longer use this method to get the rewards. However, it's still worth understanding how it worked, as it could help us piece the clues together quicker, should Wizards run a similar secret promo in future.

It might sound over-cautious, but we've had some rough moments like this in the past, and everyone's there to have fun - so think about it.
